blocks.text: The Tang dynasty (618–907), founded by Emperor Gaozu (Li Yuan), lasted 289 years under 22 emperors (including Wu Zetian) and was one of the most powerful states in the world of its day. In 618 Li Yuan compelled Emperor Gong of Sui to abdicate and founded the Tang, renaming the capital Daxing as Chang'an.

In 626 Li Shimin carried out the Xuanwu Gate Incident, killing the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Prince of Qi Li Yuanji, and then took the throne as Emperor Taizong, inaugurating the celebrated Zhenguan era. After the Eastern Turkic Khaganate fell in 630, the peoples of the north hailed Taizong as the 'Heavenly Khan'. In 641 the Tang court arranged for Princess Wencheng to marry Songtsen Gampo, the tsenpo of Tibet.

In 690 Wu Zetian deposed Emperor Ruizong and took the imperial throne herself, changing the dynastic name to Zhou (the Wu Zhou), becoming the only female emperor in Chinese history; during her reign she introduced the palace examination and the military examination. After the Shenlong coup of 705 the Tang was restored. Under Emperor Xuanzong the government was clear and able, a time known as the Kaiyuan flourishing age, and by the Tianbao era the population reached 80 million.

In 755 An Lushan launched the An Lushan Rebellion, the turning point at which the Tang shifted from prosperity to decline; in 907 Zhu Wen compelled Emperor Ai to abdicate and founded the Later Liang, ending the Tang and opening the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. To remember the Tang, hold onto three nodes: the Zhenguan era, the Kaiyuan flourishing age, and the An Lushan Rebellion.

The Hundred Schools of Thought is the later collective name for the thinkers and schools of Chinese intellectual life in the pre-Qin period. The 'Masters' include such representative figures as Laozi, Zhuangzi, Confucius, Mencius, Xunzi, Mozi, Liezi, Sunzi, Shenzi, Han Feizi, and Guiguzi.

By the late Spring and Autumn period such influential schools as Daoism, Confucianism, Mohism, the School of Names, Legalism, the School of Military Strategy, and the Yin-Yang school had appeared; by the mid-Warring States the Hundred Schools contended, and the profusion of doctrines laid a deep foundation for Chinese culture.

Sima Tan, father of Sima Qian, grouped the schools of the pre-Qin era into six: Daoism, Confucianism, Mohism, the School of Names, Legalism, and the Yin-Yang school. In the Book of Han, Ban Gu of the Eastern Han expanded this to ten schools, adding the School of Diplomacy, the School of Agrarianism, the School of Syncretism, and the School of Storytellers.

The Qin burned books and buried scholars alive, and Emperor Wu of Han dismissed the Hundred Schools and honored only Confucianism. The Hundred Schools' contention was the first great movement of intellectual liberation in Chinese history. To remember the Masters, recall the major schools — Confucianism, Daoism, Mohism, Legalism — and their foundational place in Chinese culture.

blocks.text: The Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains is the work of Huang Gongwang, a painter active at the end of the Song and the beginning of the Yuan dynasty. Painted between 1347 and 1350 against the backdrop of the Fuchun River in Zhejiang, it is his masterpiece, praised by later generations as the 'Lanting of painting' and the 'supreme divine work of landscape painting', and it is counted among China's ten greatest surviving paintings.

blocks.caption: The Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains and the Remaining Mountain Scroll

blocks.text: In the early Qing, under the Shunzhi emperor, the painting passed to Wu Hongyu. Before his death, Wu decided to have the painting buried with him, and when it was thrown into the fire, his nephew Wu Zhendu rescued it from the flames - but the scroll had been burned into two sections, one large and one small. The small opening section, repaired, is known as the 'Remaining Mountain Scroll', measuring 51.4 cm wide and 31.8 cm high, about one-fourteenth of the original; the longer section is the 'Scroll for Master Wuyong', 636.9 cm wide and 33 cm high, about twelve-fourteenths of the original.

The Zhejiang Museum treasures precisely this 'Remaining Mountain Scroll'; it, too, was chosen among the museum's top ten treasures. On 2 June 2011, the Remaining Mountain Scroll and the National Palace Museum's Scroll for Master Wuyong were shown together at the Taipei palace museum, the two originals displayed side by side in a single case sixteen metres long.

As you view the Remaining Mountain Scroll, first think of its story: a fire split the long scroll in two, one part staying in Hangzhou and one going to Taiwan - and this small section before you is where that story begins.

blocks.text: The Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms (in the strict sense, 907–960) began with the fall of the Tang and ended with the Song's reunification of most of the Chinese heartland; it was in essence a continuation of late-Tang politics and the fragmentation of military governorships. In 907 Zhu Wen, Prince of Liang, usurped the Tang and founded the Later Liang, marking the start of the period.

The Five Dynasties were the Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han, and Later Zhou. In 936 Shi Jingtang, using Khitan troops, founded the Later Jin and ceded the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun to the Khitan; in 947 Yelü Deguang changed the state name to Great Liao, formally establishing the Liao dynasty. Chai Rong, Emperor Shizong of the Later Zhou, is hailed as the finest ruler of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms.

The Ten Kingdoms comprised Wu, Southern Tang, Wuyue, and Min in the Jiangnan region; Jingnan, Chu, and Southern Han in the Huguang region; Former Shu and Later Shu in the Sichuan lands; and Northern Han, the only one in the north. In 960 Zhao Kuangyin staged the Chenqiao mutiny, deposing Emperor Gong of the Later Zhou; the Five Dynasties ended, and Zhao Kuangyin founded the Song.

In 979 Northern Han surrendered to the Song, ending the Ten Kingdoms and formally opening the Song period. To remember the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, recall the Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han, and Later Zhou; the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun; and the Chenqiao mutiny.

The An Lushan Rebellion (755–763) was a great civil war that broke out in the mid-Tang, lasting, as the sources record, over seven years. It was launched by An Lushan, military governor of three frontier commands, and his subordinate Shi Siming, who marched troops toward the capital under the banner of punishing the imperial kinsman Yang Guozhong; it spanned the reigns of Emperors Xuanzong, Suzong, and Daizong.

On the ninth day of the eleventh month in the fourteenth year of Tianbao (December 16, 755), An Lushan rose in revolt at Fanyang (present-day Beijing); on the first day of the first month of 756 he proclaimed himself emperor at Luoyang under the title Great Yan. When Xuanzong fled to Mawei Slope, his soldiers mutinied, Yang Guozhong was cut down, and Xuanzong issued an order that the imperial consort Yang Guifei be strangled. The crown prince, Li Heng, was enthroned at Lingzhou as Emperor Suzong.

In the spring of 763 (the second year of Baoying), Shi Chaoyi, with no way out, hanged himself, ending the rebellion after seven years and two months. After the war the court accepted the surrender of the rebels' remnants, appointing Tian Chengsi military governor of Weibo, Li Huaixian of Youzhou, and Li Baochen of Chengde, giving rise to the separatist rule of the Three Garrison Towns of Hebei.

The An Lushan Rebellion is regarded as the pivotal event in the Tang's shift from prosperity to decline. Although it was ultimately suppressed with the aid of the Uyghurs, the registered Han population of the Tang fell by more than half in its aftermath. To remember the rebellion, recall An Lushan and Shi Siming, Mawei Slope, and the years 755 to 763.

blocks.text: Huang Gongwang (1269-1354), courtesy name Zijiu, with the sobriquets Dachi, Dachi Daoren and Yifeng Daoren, was a Yuan-dynasty painter from Changshu Prefecture, Pingjiang Circuit (today's Changshu, Suzhou, Jiangsu). Honoured as the first of the 'Four Great Masters of the Yuan', he is named alongside Wu Zhen, Ni Zan and Wang Meng.

blocks.caption: Huang Gongwang and the Fuchun River

blocks.text: Huang Gongwang did not begin studying painting until he was fifty. Guided by Zhao Mengfu, he originated the 'light crimson' (qianjiang) landscape style, and his ink landscapes were particularly accomplished. His masterpiece is the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains, and his treatise Notes on Landscape Painting is an important theoretical work of Chinese landscape painting.

In September 1315 (the 2nd year of Yanyou), Huang Gongwang was imprisoned after being implicated in the corruption case of Zhang Lu. After his release he entered the Quanzhen Daoist order. On the 25th day of the 10th month of 1354 (the 14th year of Zhizheng), he died in Changshu and was buried at the western foot of Mount Yu.

After seeing the Remaining Mountain Scroll at the Zhejiang Museum, spare a thought for the painter who took up art at fifty yet turned the Fuchun River into the 'Lanting of painting': his humble start and late flowering are themselves a story worth reading slowly.

blocks.text: The Great Wall is the collective name for the large-scale military walls built by successive dynasties across northern China. When its eastern and western sections and its successive passes are added up, it stretches over ten thousand li (roughly 4,500 to 6,000 kilometers), which is why it is also called the 'Wall of Ten Thousand Li'. Walls were already being built in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods; the Qi wall is the earliest wall in the history of the Central Plains.

The name 'Ten Thousand Li Wall' dates only from the First Emperor: in 221 BC he unified the Central Plains by conquering the six states, and in 214 BC sent General Meng Tian with 300,000 men against the Xiongnu, taking the Hetao region and linking the old walls built by Qin, Zhao, and Yan into a line stretching ten thousand li from Lintao to Liaodong. The Western Han also built the longest wall of its kind in history, the Han Wall.

The wall as it survives today is chiefly the Ming Great Wall, begun in the 14th century and running from Jiayuguan in the west to the Hushan wall in the east. Through 20 large-scale construction campaigns the Ming built a wall stretching 8,851.8 kilometers from Jiayuguan in Gansu in the west to Hushan in Liaoning in the east. The wall system consists chiefly of four parts: passes, walls and towers, and beacon towers.

In 1987 the Great Wall was inscribed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site. In the Tang, since the Turks had been pacified under Emperor Taizong, no wall was built for the next three hundred years, and the Qing never built on it until its fall. To remember the Great Wall, recall that it began in the Spring and Autumn period, was named under the First Emperor, and survives today mostly as the Ming Wall.

Chinese history conventionally runs from the age of legend all the way to the end of the imperial system. The Origins of Chinese Civilization research project holds that around 5,800 years ago, marked social stratification appeared one after another across several regions of China, an accelerating phase in the beginnings of civilization; after roughly 3,800 years ago, the Central Plains, exemplified by the Erlitou culture, entered the dynastic age, as early broad-based states ruled by royal power gradually took shape.

The major dynasties of Chinese history are traditionally ordered as Xia, Shang, Zhou, Qin, Han, the Three Kingdoms, the Western and Eastern Jin, the Northern and Southern Dynasties, Sui, Tang, the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, Song, Yuan, Ming and Qing: the Xia existed roughly from 2070 to 1600 BC; the Shang was founded around 1600 BC; the Zhou lasted about eight hundred years, from King Wu's conquest of the Shang in 1046 BC to the Qin's destruction of the Eastern Zhou royal house in 256 BC; and the Qin (221–207 BC) was the first unified, centrally governed empire in Chinese history.

The discovery of oracle bone inscriptions at Yinxu from the late Shang brought China into a stage of verifiable history supported by mature written materials; a continuously dated written record conventionally begins with the first year of the Gonghe regency of the Western Zhou in 841 BC. In 221 BC, Qin Shi Huang unified the six states, establishing the imperial institution and the commandery-county system, and standardizing script, weights and measures, and the legal code.

In 1911 the Xinhai Revolution overthrew the Qing dynasty, and in 1912 the Republic of China was founded, ending the imperial monarchy that had lasted more than two thousand years. To remember the dynasties, first recite them in order — Xia, Shang, Zhou, Qin, Han; Three Kingdoms, Western and Eastern Jin, Northern and Southern Dynasties; Sui, Tang, Five Dynasties, Song, Yuan, Ming, Qing — then fill in the approximate dates of each.
Tea has been drunk in China for thousands of years. In the Tang dynasty, Lu Yu's Classic of Tea turned growing, brewing, and tasting into a coherent art form.
Fine tea is traditionally paired with fine spring water, which is why tea terraces and springs around West Lake, such as Longjing and Hupao, are celebrated as cultural landscapes in their own right.

The Qing dynasty (1636 or 1644–1912), whose official title was the Great Qing, was the unified dynasty founded by the Manchus and the last imperial dynasty in Chinese history; it had 11 emperors from the time Hong Taiji fixed the name Great Qing. In 1616 Nurhaci founded the Later Jin khanate, and in 1636 Hong Taiji proclaimed himself emperor at Shengjing and changed the dynastic name to Great Qing.

In 1644 Li Zicheng took Beijing and the Ming fell; that same year Wu Sangui let the Qing forces through the pass, an event known as the Jiashen Transition, and the Qing army moved its capital to Beijing. Under the successive reigns of Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong the Qing entered the High Qing era; at its peak the territory it effectively controlled reached 13.1 million square kilometers.

The Kangxi emperor reigned for sixty-one years and ten months, the longest reign in Chinese history; the Yongzheng emperor established the Grand Council to strengthen imperial authority. After the Opium War of 1840, China entered its modern age, as the Taiping Rebellion, the Self-Strengthening Movement, and the Hundred Days' Reform followed in turn.

In 1911 the Wuchang Uprising broke out and the Xinhai Revolution overthrew the Qing; on February 12, 1912, the Empress Dowager Longyu issued an abdication edict in the name of the emperor Puyi, and the Qing formally came to an end, closing more than two thousand years of imperial monarchy. To remember the Qing, recall the High Qing era of Kangxi, Yongzheng, and Qianlong; the Opium War; and the Xinhai Revolution's end of the imperial system.

blocks.text: The Three Kingdoms (in the strict sense, 220–280 AD) was a period in which the states of Wei, Shu Han, and Wu stood side by side, with its prelude traced to the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184. In 200 Cao Cao defeated Yuan Shao, the strongest power of the north, at the Battle of Guandu; in 208 he was in turn defeated by the allied forces of Sun Quan and Liu Bei at the Battle of Red Cliffs, taking the first step toward the tripartite standoff.

Cao Cao died in 220, and that same year his son Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian of Han, taking the dynastic name 'Wei' — historically styled Cao Wei. The Eastern Han thus came to an end and the Three Kingdoms period formally began. In 221 Liu Bei proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu under the name 'Han', styled Shu Han; and in 229 Sun Quan formally took the title of emperor under the name 'Wu', styled Sun Wu.

In 263 Sima Zhao launched a campaign against Shu and Shu Han fell; in 265 Sima Yan accepted the abdication of Emperor Yuan of Wei and proclaimed himself emperor under the name 'Jin', styled the Western Jin, and Cao Wei perished; in 280 the Western Jin conquered Wu, bringing the Three Kingdoms period to an end.

During the Three Kingdoms, Cao Wei replaced the Han's system of recommendation with the Nine Ranks system, producing a situation in which 'the upper ranks had no families of humble origin and the lower ranks no great clans'. The Records of the Three Kingdoms, written by Chen Shou with annotations by Pei Songzhi, is one of the highly regarded 'Former Four Histories' among the Twenty-Four Histories, and the Romance of the Three Kingdoms by Luo Guanzhong became one of China's Four Great Classical Novels. To remember the Three Kingdoms, recall 'Wei, Shu, and Wu; Guandu; Red Cliffs'.

In June 2009, to mark the 80th anniversary of its founding, the Zhejiang Museum launched a 'Top Ten Treasures' selection. Over the course of one month, a combination of visitor votes and expert opinion produced a list of the ten most representative artefacts in the collection.

blocks.caption: The Selection of the Top Ten Treasures

blocks.text: The ten treasures chosen were: the Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue (Warring States period); the Ten-Thousand-Work Sedan Chair (Republic of China era); the gilded silver Asoka Pagoda of Wuyue (Five Dynasties period); the Liangzhu culture jade cong; the Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi' (The Phoenix Sings in Color); Huang Gongwang's 'Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains (Remaining Mountain Scroll)' (Yuan dynasty); the Spring and Autumn bronze house of musicians; the Hemudu culture ivory carving of twin birds facing the sun; the Yuan Longquan kiln boat-shaped water dropper; and the painted clay standing bodhisattva of the Northern Song dynasty.

Spanning from the Neolithic Hemudu and Liangzhu cultures to the Republican era, these ten objects are a microcosm of the museum's collection system: jade, porcelain, lacquer, painting and calligraphy, bronze, ivory carving and clay sculpture - categories of every kind.
Treat this list as a self-guided route: hunt them down one by one through the galleries, and with each one you find, you understand a little more of Zhejiang's craft and history.

blocks.text: The Zhou was the hereditary dynasty that succeeded the Shang, divided into the Western Zhou (1046–771 BC) and the Eastern Zhou (770–256 BC). The Western Zhou was founded when King Wu overthrew the Shang, with its capital at Haojing; the Eastern Zhou was based at Luoyi (present-day Luoyang, Henan).

After conquering the Shang, King Wu instituted a system of enfeoffment, enfeofing royal kinsmen and meritorious ministers in the east to serve as shields for the royal house. In 841 BC the People's Riot broke out in Haojing, and King Li fled to Zhi; the ensuing regency is known as the Gonghe interregnum. Its first year, 841 BC, marks the beginning of clear, unbroken reign-year dating in Chinese history.

King You deposed his queen, the daughter of the Marquis of Western Shen, and the crown prince Yijiu, installing Bao Si as queen and her son Bofu as heir. In 771 BC the Quanrong tribes killed King You at Mount Li, an event known as the Quanrong Disaster, and the Western Zhou perished. In 770 BC King Ping moved the capital east to Luoyi, an event recorded as the Eastern Move of King Ping, marking the beginning of the Eastern Zhou.

During the Eastern Zhou the king's authority steadily declined: Duke Huan of Qi, Duke Xiang of Song, Duke Wen of Jin, Duke Mu of Qin, and King Zhuang of Chu rose in turn, remembered in the Records of the Grand Historian as the Five Hegemons of the Spring and Autumn period. Thereafter came the Partition of Jin among three houses and the Tian family's replacement of the Jiang clan in Qi, until Qin finally unified the six states. To remember the Zhou, recall three events — enfeoffment, the first Gonghe year, and King Ping's eastern move — and the Western and Eastern Zhou join into a single line.

blocks.text: Sha Menghai (11 June 1900 - 10 October 1992), originally named Sha Wenruo, courtesy name Menghai, with the sobriquets Shacun, Lansha, Shihuang and Jueming, came from Sha village in Tangxi township, Yin County, Zhejiang (today's Yinzhou District, Ningbo). He was a Chinese calligrapher and seal carver, and a master whose ties to the Zhejiang Museum ran deep.

blocks.caption: Sha Menghai and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: In August 1953, Sha Menghai concurrently served as head of the history department of the Zhejiang Museum. One account has him becoming honorary director of the museum in August 1984; another source says he became honorary director in 1981, the same year he was elected vice-chairman of the Chinese Calligraphers Association. He also became a professor of calligraphy and seal carving at the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts in 1963, was elected director of the Xiling Seal Art Society in 1979, served as head of the Xiling Academy of Calligraphy and Painting in 1980, and was made a lifetime professor of the academy in 1989.

The former residence of Sha Menghai stands at No. 15 Longyou Road, Hangzhou, covering 870 square metres with a total floor area of 601 square metres, a two-storey villa of brick-and-timber construction. The five-character plaque reading 'Former Residence of Sha Menghai' in the courtyard was written by the seal carver and calligrapher Qian Juntao. It formally opened in November 2004.

When you visit the Zhejiang Museum and see its collection of calligraphy and seals, of which Sha Menghai is a representative figure, spare a thought for his ties to the Xiling Seal Art Society and to Gushan - calligraphy, seal carving and the cultural institutions of Zhejiang are joined together in him.

blocks.text: Chinese civilization is commonly regarded as some five thousand years old. The Origins of Chinese Civilization research project holds that around 5,800 years ago, marked social stratification appeared one after another across several regions of China, marking an accelerating phase in the origins of civilization.

blocks.caption: Five Thousand Years of Chinese Civilization

blocks.text: The project divides the period from roughly 5,800 to 3,800 years ago into the age of ancient states, followed by the dynastic age represented by sites such as Erlitou. From around 3,800 years ago onward, the Central Plains, exemplified by the Erlitou culture, entered the dynastic age, as early broad-based states under royal power gradually took shape.

Archeologically, the Liangzhu ancient city site, dated to roughly 3300–2300 BC, reveals monumental earthen architecture, urban planning, water management systems, rice agriculture, a system of jade ritual objects, and hierarchical differentiation in burials — tangible evidence of the early stage of Chinese civilization.

By traditional dating the Xia is generally placed between 2070 and 1600 BC. To remember the five thousand years of Chinese civilization, recall the origins research project, the progression from the age of ancient states to the dynastic age, and the Liangzhu evidence.

blocks.text: The Yaoshan site lies about 5 kilometres northeast of the ancient Liangzhu city, covering about 66.56 hectares. At its centre is a square altar aligned exactly north–south, used for major rituals; after the altar fell out of use, the place became a high-ranking aristocratic cemetery.

The Yaoshan cemetery began as an altar 20 metres square and 2 metres high, from whose surface twelve jade-bearing tombs were cleared. The tombs lie south of the altar in two rows — seven in the southern row and six in the northern — all rectangular shaft graves with heads facing due south. The Yaoshan cemetery may also be connected with astronomical observation and calendar-keeping.

The beast-mask motif of Liangzhu is closely tied to this altar: jade cong, beast masks and the altar together proclaim the theocratic character of Liangzhu. Like Fanshan, the Yaoshan site was named among China's Top Ten Archaeological Discoveries of the Seventh Five-Year Plan period in February 1989.

At the Yaoshan altar, first look at the square platform and the tomb pits aligned to the south, then consider its transformation from 'altar to cemetery' — a space where sacred authority and power intertwine takes shape before you.

Buddhism entered China from India around the turn of the common era and gradually blended with Confucian and Daoist thought. Temples, pagodas, and grotto carvings became fixtures of the Chinese landscape.
Chinese Buddhist temples are not just places of worship; their bells, pagodas, and mountain settings shaped a contemplative aesthetic you will meet at sites like Lingyin and Jingci.

The Zhenguan Rule refers to the clear and able government of Emperor Taizong of Tang during his 23-year reign (627–649). In those twenty-three years he used a single era name, Zhenguan, hence the name; it was the first golden age of the Tang.

Emperor Taizong appointed talented men and welcomed frank remonstrance, giving high office to Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Wei Zheng, and others; Wei Zheng offered more than two hundred pieces of remonstrance in all. After Wei Zheng's death, the emperor reflected: 'Use bronze as a mirror to straighten one's dress; use the past as a mirror to understand the rise and fall of states; use a person as a mirror to see what is gained and lost.'

Economically, Taizong implemented the equal-field land system and the taxation of rent, levy, and service, cutting extravagance and easing burdens. Abroad, he subdued in turn the Eastern Turks, the Xueyantuo, Gaochang, and Tuyuhun, and established the Anxi Protectorate in the Western Regions; the peoples of the northwest jointly honored him as the Heavenly Khan.

The Zhenguan Rule laid vital groundwork for the later Kaiyuan flourishing age. To remember it, recall the single era name used for 23 years, the ministers Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, and Wei Zheng, and the title Heavenly Khan.

Buddhism was a central part of Wuyue culture, and every king of Wuyue was a devout believer. By the reign of King Zhongyi the kingdom boasted 84,000 stupas and pagodas, including such famous ones as Hangzhou's Baochu Pagoda and Leifeng Pagoda today.

blocks.caption: Wuyue Buddhism and the Jewel Casket Stupa

blocks.text: The jewel casket stupa - also called the 'baogieyin ta', the gold-painted tower or the Asoka pagoda - is a type of solid tower, square in plan, made up of four parts: a base, a body, an eave and a spire. The eaves turn up at the four corners of the body in what is called the 'mountain-flower banana-leaf' (shanhua jiaoye) form. The type developed from the ancient Indian stupa and entered China via Nepal.

In the Five Dynasties period, King Qian Hongchu of Wuyue, imitating King Asoka, had 84,000 pagodas built, spreading the jewel casket stupa widely and leaving behind many remains. Under Wuyue's Buddhist atmosphere, block printing in Hangzhou flourished; in the reign of King Zhongyi (Qian Chu) alone, as many as 662,000 scrolls of sutras and images of Buddhas were printed.

When you see a jewel casket stupa such as the gilded silver Asoka Pagoda in the gallery, first look at the four 'mountain-flower banana-leaf' corners of the crown, then think of the Wuyue king who 'built 84,000 pagodas' - a small stupa holds the shadow of an entire Buddhist kingdom.

blocks.text: The Rule of Wen and Jing refers to the reigns of Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing of Han — a period of good governance and the first golden age of a unified dynasty in Chinese history. It laid the foundations on which Emperor Wu later carried the Han to its peak.

Early in the Han, the economy was weak, and the court espoused the Huang-Lao arts of government, adopting policies of light levies and letting the people rest. In the second year of Emperor Wen's reign (178 BC) and the twelfth (168 BC), the land tax was halved on each occasion, eventually settled at one-thirtieth, and in the thirteenth year of his reign it was abolished altogether.

Emperor Wen lived frugally, adding nothing to his palaces, carriages, and wardrobe, and issued edicts forbidding the commanderies and kingdoms from presenting rare treasures. In the early years of his reign Emperor Jing put down the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms, then devoted himself to government, maintaining a policy of marriage alliance with the Xiongnu.

The histories say that the capital's coins piled up by the tens of millions, their strings rotted beyond counting, and that the grain of the great granaries, laid up year after year, overflowed and rotted in the open. To remember the Rule of Wen and Jing, recall light levies, the one-thirtieth tax, and the non-intervention of Huang-Lao governance.

The Liangzhu culture spread across the Lake Tai region in the lower Yangtze, covering a total cultural area of about 36,500 square kilometres, of which plains account for about five-sixths. The density of waterways averages 3 to 4 kilometres per square kilometre.

blocks.caption: Distribution around Lake Tai and the Site Cluster

blocks.text: Liangzhu's core area was the region around Lake Tai: bounded by Hangzhou Bay and the northern bank of the Qiantang River to the south, extending its influence over the Ningshao Plain, reaching the sea to the east, and stopping at the Maoshan and Tianmu mountains near Zhenjiang to the west. To the north it crossed the Yangtze, reaching northern Jiangsu at its peak. In the middle period of the Liangzhu culture, the Liangzhu site cluster on the south shore of Lake Tai was dominant; later, the centre of power shifted north of the lake to the Sidun site cluster in the Changzhou area.

The Liangzhu site cluster consists roughly of three tiers of settlements: one first-tier settlement, the Mojiaoshan site; nine second-tier settlements of 30,000–90,000 square metres; and more than thirty third-tier settlements each under 20,000 square metres. At Longnan, Meiyan, in Wujiang, Jiangsu, an early village covering 20,000 square metres contains twelve houses and eighteen burials.
When visiting the sites or an exhibition, keep 'around Lake Tai' as your frame of reference: every piece of jade and every earthen terrace you see comes from this water-networked plain of Lake Tai.

blocks.text: The Kangxi emperor (1654–1722), personal name Xuanye of the Aisin Gioro clan, reigned from 1661 to 1722 under the era name Kangxi, with the temple name Shengzu. The third son of the Shunzhi emperor, Xuanye ascended the throne in 1661 upon his father's death, at only eight years old by Chinese reckoning.

In the eighth year of Kangxi (1669), the emperor had the young palace attendants seize Oboi on charges of disrespect, thereby fully recovering control of the court. In 1673, when the Kangxi emperor decided to abolish the feudatories, the Prince of Pingxi, Wu Sangui, rose against the Qing, and the Revolt of the Three Feudatories was finally crushed in 1681.

In 1683 the Kangxi emperor appointed Shi Lang admiral of the Fujian fleet; Shi Lang took Penghu, Zheng Keshuang surrendered, and Taiwan was pacified. The emperor also signed the Treaty of Nerchinsk with Russia, securing control of the Amur basin and the vast northeast. From 1690 to 1697 he repeatedly defeated Galdan of the Dzungar confederation, in campaigns remembered as the Three Expeditions against Galdan.

The Kangxi emperor reigned for sixty-one years and ten months, the longest reign in Chinese history. To remember him, recall the seizure of Oboi, the suppression of the Three Feudatories, the recovery of Taiwan, and the Three Expeditions against Galdan.

blocks.text: The Liangzhu culture, dating from around 5300 to 4000 years ago, is one of China's Neolithic archaeological cultures. It arose and flourished in the Lake Tai region of the lower Yangtze River, where more than 500 sites have been found. Centred on Mojiaoshan near the Liangzhu site, it is regarded as one of the cradles of prehistoric Chinese civilization.

The most distinctive feature of the Liangzhu culture is the use of jade for ritual and burial, including large cong tubes, bi discs and yue axes. Among them, the jade cong shows the finest craftsmanship and the greatest authority: it is often carved with delicate beast masks regarded as images of deities, while the jade yue symbolizes military and royal power. The Liangzhu people skillfully cultivated with stone plows, rice began to become the staple food source, and early forms of writing appeared.

Liangzhu's political organization has been described as a chiefdom, and some scholars believe it had already taken the embryonic form of a state. It could mobilize large numbers of laborers to build great ritual grounds, city walls and flood-control embankments, and its society was stratified into an aristocracy and commoners. The Liangzhu culture disappeared around 4000 years ago; the succeeding Maqiao culture shows a marked decline in agricultural economy, jade working and settlement patterns.

When viewing Liangzhu artefacts, let your eye rest on the forms of the cong, bi and yue and their beast-mask motifs. From one jade object after another, you can read a prehistoric society skilled at organizing labour and devoted to jade ritual.

Confucius (551–479 BC), personal name Qiu and courtesy name Zhongni, of the Kong lineage, was a Lu state official, thinker, and educator of the Spring and Autumn period. He was the founder of Confucian thought and the founder of Chinese philosophy and ethics. He was born in 551 BC at Zouyi, near Qufu in the state of Lu.

Confucius pioneered education for the common people, holding that education should be offered to all without distinction, and taught in accordance with each student's ability. He is said to have had three thousand disciples, of whom seventy-two mastered the six arts. His way of governing put moral cultivation of the people first, advocating rule by virtue and the virtues of benevolence (ren), filial piety, loyalty, and reciprocity.

His disciples compiled the Analects, recording Confucius's words and deeds. Benevolence (ren) is the heart of his thought, appearing in 58 of the Analects' more than 400 chapters. Confucius taught the six arts of ritual, music, archery, charioteering, calligraphy, and mathematics, and edited the Five Classics, yet he 'transmitted rather than created', leaving behind no works of his own.

His school revered him as a sage, and successive courts honored him as the 'model teacher for ten thousand generations'. To remember Confucius, recall benevolence, education for all, the Analects, and the six arts.

On 6 July 2019, the archaeological ruins of Liangzhu city, meeting UNESCO World Heritage criteria (iii) and (iv), were inscribed on the World Heritage List — a holy site attesting to more than five thousand years of Chinese civilization.

blocks.caption: World Heritage: Proof of Five Thousand Years of Civilization

blocks.text: The Liangzhu site was placed on China's Tentative List for World Cultural Heritage in 1994, designated a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level (fourth batch) in 1996, and named among the first national archaeological site parks in 2010. It was formally inscribed on the World Heritage List on 6 July 2019; since 2020, 6 July each year — the anniversary of the inscription — has been celebrated as 'Hangzhou Liangzhu Day'.

The World Heritage Committee's rationale: Liangzhu is an outstanding testimony to an early regional state of the late Neolithic in China, founded on rice agriculture and marked by social stratification and unified belief, and it demonstrates in outstanding fashion the political transition from Neolithic societies to large, integrated political entities.

When you visit Liangzhu, you will often hear of 'five thousand years of civilization'. This is not a slogan but the formal recognition UNESCO has given this watery landscape of sites. The ground beneath your feet is in dialogue with the very source of Chinese civilization.

blocks.text: The Xia dynasty existed roughly from 2070 to 1600 BC and is the first hereditary dynastic state of the Central Plains recorded in Chinese history. According to historical records, Yu passed the throne to his son Qi, replacing the primitive practice of abdicating to a worthy successor; governance by a shared public realm gave way to rule passed down within one family, inaugurating nearly four thousand years of hereditary monarchy in China.

The Xia is said to have passed through fourteen reigns and seventeen kings of the Si clan, with a duration sometimes given as 470 years, before being overthrown by the Shang. The sources also contain famous episodes such as 'Taikang Loses the State' and 'Shaokang's Restoration': Taikang neglected government for pleasure, and Yi, the leader of the Youqiong tribe of the eastern Yi peoples, seized the Xia government with the backing of the Xia people; Shaokang later defeated Hanzhuo's forces and restored the Xia realm.

Archeologically, the Erlitou site in western Henan and southern Shanxi broadly matches the dating and location expected of Xia culture, and many historians at home and abroad consider that the full sequence, or the first two phases, of the Erlitou site at Yanshi may be the remains of a Xia capital. Yet no contemporary written records like the oracle-bone divination texts of Yinxu have ever been unearthed, so the existence and precise dates of the Xia remain debated.

To remember the Xia, keep three keywords in mind: 'roughly 2070–1600 BC', 'hereditary dynasty', and 'the unresolved Erlitou site'. It is both the beginning of the dynastic chain and a key to understanding where China's verifiable history begins.

The state of Yue was one of the principal sources of smelting materials such as copper and tin in the pre-Qin period. That the Yue people excelled at making swords and blades was a universally acknowledged fact before the Western Han. Works such as the Rites of Zhou, the Zhuangzi, the Strategies of the Warring States and the Huainanzi all praise the quality of Yue weapons. Yue also boasted the renowned swordmaker Ou Yezi and the sword connoisseur Xue Zhu.

blocks.caption: The Bronze Sword Tradition of the Yue State

blocks.text: The 'Artificers' Record' of the Rites of Zhou notes that 'the swords of Wu and Yue... cannot be made as fine anywhere else', and the Zhuangzi likewise says, 'The swords of Gan and Yue are kept in their scabbards and not dared to be used - they are treasured above all.' So precious were the swords of Wu and Yue in their day. The Sword of King Goujian of Yue unearthed today has been shown to use a copper-sulfide anti-corrosion technique - the Yue people had already mastered composite-metal craftsmanship.

Unlike the central plain states, which emphasized chariot warfare, the southern states of Wu and Yue fought mostly in close-order infantry battles, and infantry made up the core of the Yue army. Bronze objects of Yue unearthed in modern times - the Sword of King Goujian and the Sword of King Zhejiyushi - bear this tradition out.

As you stand before the Yue sword case, look closely at the inscriptions and the colour of the bronze on the blades - behind a sword 'treasured above all' lies the whole bronze-casting tradition of Wu and Yue.

blocks.text: The King Jade Cong was excavated from Tomb 12 at Fanshan. Weighing 3,500 grams and carved with delicate beast-mask motifs, it is regarded as the 'King of Cong' for being the supreme example of Liangzhu jade in both size and craftsmanship. It is a national treasure jointly presented by the Liangzhu Museum and the Zhejiang Provincial Museum.

The cong is a ritual object used to worship the earth, square on the outside and hollow-cylindrical within. The densely carved beast-mask decoration of the King Jade Cong shows the exquisite craftsmanship of Liangzhu jade, in which 'three incised lines may pass within a single millimetre'. For this very reason, such objects must have been made by full-time, even hereditary craftsmen released from agricultural labour.

The King Jade Cong is on the list of cultural relics prohibited from travelling abroad for exhibition, and has been shown in displays such as Zhejiang across Ten Thousand Years. It embodies, in concentrated form, the jade ritual system and theocratic character of Liangzhu.

When viewing the King Jade Cong, first take in its sheer weight and its square-outside, round-within form, then study the beast-mask motifs covering its surface. It is at once the summit of craft and an object of power, connecting heaven and earth, placed in a leader's tomb.

blocks.text: The jade yue was modelled on the stone yue battle-axe. In Liangzhu it symbolized military and royal power, ranking among aristocratic tomb jades second only to the cong.

blocks.caption: The Jade Yue and Royal Authority

blocks.text: A superbly made jade yue from Tomb 12 at Fanshan, regarded as the 'King of Yue', has a 70–80 cm wooden haft inset with jade beads and fitted with jade finials at both ends; the blade is set transversely into the haft. It is a symbol of military and royal power.

Liangzhu's polity was a chiefdom or early state capable of mobilizing great numbers of workers. The military power represented by the yue ran parallel to the theocratic power of the cong, forming the twin pillars of Liangzhu's system of authority.

When you find the jade yue in the galleries, first study its blade and the drilled holes, then imagine it mounted on its jade-studded wooden haft. This object is not merely a declaration of power but direct evidence of the bearer's status.

blocks.text: The Jingkang Incident, also called the Humiliation of Jingkang, refers to the great war of 1125–1127 in which the Jurchens captured Bianliang (present-day Kaifeng, Henan), the capital of the Northern Song, and carried off Emperor Qinzong, the retired Emperor Huizong, nearly the entire imperial clan of the Song Taizong line, consorts, officials, and more than a hundred thousand residents of the capital.

The capital fell on the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary eleventh month of the first year of Jingkang (January 9, 1127), which is how the incident got its name. In the first month of 1126 the eastern Jin army reached the walls of Kaifeng but failed to break in, thanks to the stout defense organized by the capital's defender Li Gang; in the autumn of 1126 the Jin attacked again on two fronts and, after besieging the city for a month, breached it.

In the spring of 1127 the Jin carried the two emperors Huizong and Qinzong and a great number of the Song Taizong imperial clan northward; on the sixth day of the second month of the second year of Jingkang (March 20, 1127), the Jin emperor decreed that the two deposed rulers become commoners, and the Northern Song (960–1127) came to an end.

After the fall of the Northern Song, Prince Kang, Zhao Gou, proclaimed himself emperor at Yingtian Prefecture as Emperor Gaozong, beginning the Southern Song; in 1141 the Song and Jin signed the Treaty of Shaoxing, fixing the boundary along the Qinling Mountains and the Huai River. To remember the Jingkang Incident, recall the year 1127, the fall of Bianjing, and the capture of Emperors Huizong and Qinzong.

blocks.text: The god-man beast mask (also called simply the beast-mask motif) is the most classic design on Liangzhu jade. Often carved on the faces of cong, yue and jade ornaments, it is regarded as the 'image of the spirit' of Liangzhu.

The beast mask has owl-like, oval eyes with inner and outer corners drooping downward, a head shaped like an inverted trapezoid crowned with a spreading feather headdress. A small number of these motifs combine a human face with a beast mask, expressing the 'union of man and beast'. The workmanship is extraordinarily fine — in places three incised lines pass within a single millimetre.

Hayashi Minao believed the beast mask on the cong represented a sun god or fire god — the worship of the sun being linked to rice regions, where the grain depends on the sun's light and warmth — and that the feather headdress stands for birds' wings and the sun's rays. Li Xueqin, by contrast, held the mask to be a dragon. The motif shares many features with the taotie of Shang bronzes.

When you look at the god-man beast mask, first find the drooping eye corners and the spreading feather headdress, then consider how this 'image of the spirit' recurs on jade cong. It is the most direct imprint of Liangzhu's theocratic power on its artefacts.

The Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal runs from the confluence of five rivers at Tongzhou, Beijing, in the north to Hangzhou in the south, passing through Beijing, Tianjin, Hebei, Shandong, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang. It links the five great river systems of the Hai, Yellow, Huai, Yangtze, and Qiantang, and measures 1,794 kilometers in length.

The origins of the Grand Canal reach back to the end of the Spring and Autumn period: in 486 BC King Fuchai of Wu built Hancheng and cut a canal to Mokou, linking the Yangtze and the Huai; later known as the Hangou, it is the earliest stretch of the Grand Canal with a firmly dated beginning. After the Sui reunified north and south, several sections of canal centering on Luoyang were dug, known in history as the north-south Grand Canal, about 2,700 kilometers long.

The Yuan emperor Kublai rebuilt the canal on the foundations of the Sui-Tang waterway, cutting straight through its bends; the Yuan astronomer Guo Shoujing oversaw the digging of the Tonghui River. With these major works complete, the Grand Canal took the form it has today. In 2014 the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal was inscribed on the World Heritage List as part of the Grand Canal.

After the Yellow River changed course in 1855, the canal's Shandong section gradually silted up and fell out of use; in 1911 the Tianjin–Pukou Railway opened throughout, and from then on the Grand Canal and the cities along it lost their former importance. To remember the Grand Canal, recall that it runs from Tongzhou, Beijing, to Hangzhou, links five river systems, and stretches 1,794 kilometers.

blocks.text: The Republican-era ten-thousand-work sedan chair is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. It is the most magnificent and massive item of dowry in the shili hongzhuang marriage custom of the Ningbo-Shaoxing region.

Dowries in Ninghai custom centre on vermilion-and-gold woodcarving, giving rise to the saying of the 'thousand-work bed and ten-thousand-work sedan chair'. The bridal sedan was often built of woods such as catalpa, camphor and ginkgo - light yet tough - and covered with carvings of auspicious and festive motifs. It is a representative work of the vermilion-and-gold woodcarving craft.

The term 'ten-thousand-work' is a way of saying that an extraordinary number of man-hours went into it. When you look at this sedan chair, move close to study the dense layers of carved figures and auspicious patterns on its body, then step back to take in the whole silhouette and imagine a crimson trousseau procession stretching for ten li.

Emperor Wu of Han, Liu Che (156–87 BC), reigned from 141 to 87 BC, a total of 54 years. The tenth son of Emperor Jing (Liu Qi), he was made crown prince at seven and ascended the throne at sixteen. During his reign era names were first used for dating, with Jianyuan the first in Chinese history.

In the second year of Yuanshuo (127 BC), adopting the advice of Zhufu Yan, Emperor Wu issued the Order of Grace to split the kingdoms of the feudal lords into smaller states. The system of recommendatory appointment (chaju) was established from the first year of Yuanguang (134 BC), and in the fifth year of Yuanshuo (124 BC) he founded the Imperial Academy. Economically he made salt and iron state monopolies, placing officials at the production sites to control output and sale.

Emperor Wu dispatched Zhang Qian to the Western Regions, opening the channel of exchange between the Central Plains and the western lands — the Silk Road. From the sixth year of Yuanguang (129 BC) he campaigned against the Xiongnu, deploying such famed generals as Wei Qing and Huo Qubing to strike back, and established the four commanderies of Jiuquan, Wuwei, Zhangye, and Dunhuang to open the Hexi Corridor.

In the first year of Zhenghe (92 BC) the witchcraft crisis erupted, and Crown Prince Liu Ju, defeated in the ensuing conflict, took his own life; in the fourth year of Zhenghe (89 BC) the emperor issued the Luntai Edict acknowledging his errors and largely ceased military campaigns. To remember Emperor Wu, recall the Order of Grace, Zhang Qian's missions to the Western Regions, the campaigns against the Xiongnu, and the salt-and-iron monopoly.

blocks.text: The ancient Liangzhu city site is the most important and representative site of the Liangzhu culture, hailed as 'China's first city' and 'proof of five thousand years of Chinese civilization'. The city itself is the core of the site, composed of a palatial zone, an inner city and an outer city, covering 881.45 hectares.

blocks.caption: The Ancient Liangzhu City and Its Walls

blocks.text: The palatial zone covers about 0.39 square kilometres, comprising the Mojiaoshan terrace at the centre of the inner city and, to its south, the Huangfenshan and Chizhongsi terraces. The inner city is a rounded rectangle of about 300 hectares, enclosed by walls roughly 20 to 60 metres wide. The outer city covers about 500 hectares, made up of seventeen discontinuous artificial terraces, with the height of the construction descending gradually from the palatial zone through the inner city to the outer city.

Mojiaoshan, Fanshan and some small sites around them are enclosed by rammed-earth walls covering a total of 2.9 million square metres. North of the walls, a long embankment runs parallel to the Tianmu mountains: 5 kilometres long and 20–50 metres wide, built partly of rammed earth and partly of sand and cobbles. Some archaeologists believe this wall was for flood control.

As you view the walls in the site park, imagine them as the engineering boundary of five thousand years ago: the outer city, the inner city and palaces narrow inward tier by tier, and a whole order is encoded in the rising heights of the terraces.

blocks.text: The Liangzhu culture had a theocratic system. Social status was differentiated into an aristocracy and commoners, a key sign that Liangzhu had taken on the shape of an 'early state'.

Liangzhu's polity has been called a chiefdom, and some scholars believe an embryonic state had already emerged. It could mobilize large numbers of workers to build ritual grounds, city walls and flood-control embankments. Theocratic in character, religion was a vital pillar of the running of Liangzhu society.

Social stratification is also visible in the rules for using jade. The jade from the great tombs of Fanshan and Yaoshan is genuine nephrite; at Fuquanshan genuine jade predominates but is mixed with substitutes; and at Heye Di in Haining genuine and imitation jade are used roughly half and half. The tomb owners at Fanshan and Yaoshan were the top aristocracy, while the sixteen tombs found at Heye Di belonged to a lesser aristocracy, with burial jades inferior in both quantity and quality.

As you look at the jades from the tombs, mentally rank them by real versus substitute jade and by the gulf between aristocrats and commoners. The social pyramid beneath Liangzhu's theocracy then becomes self-evident.

blocks.text: The Shang dynasty was founded around 1600 BC and was replaced by the Zhou around 1046 BC, lasting more than five hundred years. Because written records from the time survive to this day, it is also the earliest dynasty belonging to the verifiable historical period of China. The oracle bone script and bronze inscriptions that appeared under the Shang are the earliest writing found in China.

Around 1300 BC, Pan Geng moved the capital to Yin (present-day Anyang, Henan), after which the Shang did not shift its capital again for more than 250 years, entering the relatively stable late-Shang period. The Shang established a system of inner and outer service regions, and the Shang king concentrated military, religious, and clan authority in his own hands.

The most representative craft of the Shang era was bronze casting; the Houmuwu ding, weighing 875 kilograms, is considered a masterpiece of ancient China and indeed of the ancient world. The Shang used cowrie shells as currency, and copper shells appeared in its late period, pioneering metal coinage. The Shang and New Kingdom Egypt were the two largest states in the world at the time.

Di Xin, the last Shang ruler, burned himself to death after being defeated by King Wu of Zhou at the Battle of Muye. To remember the Shang, keep its three hallmarks: oracle bone inscriptions, bronze vessels, and Pan Geng's move to Yin.

The jade bi is a flat jade disc with a circular hole in the centre. Alongside the cong, it is one of the most important ritual objects of Liangzhu, and it often appears together with cong in sacrifice and burial.

The bi was used in sacrifice and to ward off evil, and it was also a symbol of wealth. In Liangzhu tombs it commonly appears together with cong and yue — for example, the great tomb at Sidun, Wujin, Jiangsu, contained 124 grave goods, including 33 jade cong and 24 jade bi. The ancients honoured heaven with round bi discs.
Some Liangzhu bi discs are plain and unadorned; others carry bird motifs or solemn, complex designs resembling clan emblems, reflecting the varied yet institutionalized uses of Liangzhu jade.

When you see a bi, note the contrast between its circle and the square of the cong beside it — 'round bi for heaven, square cong for earth'. This paired set of ritual jades is a corner of the Liangzhu people's cosmology.

The imperial examination (keju) was a system for selecting officials through competitive examinations. Originating in China, it spread to other countries of the Chinese-character cultural sphere and directly gave rise to a scholar-official class chosen by examination regardless of family background. The system began in the Sui in 605, first conceived by Emperor Wen and implemented by Emperor Yang, matured and was systematized during the Tang and the Wu Zhou, and continued until the end of the Qing.

In the first year of the Daye era (605), Emperor Yang of Sui established the jinshi examination to select officials, and this became the imperial examination as later known. The Tang was the first dynasty to implement the examination on a systematic, large scale; it was divided into the regular examination (changke) and the special examination (zhike). Under Wu Zetian the palace examination, presided over by the emperor to verify the credentials of successful candidates, and the military examination for selecting generals were both pioneered.

In the Ming and Qing dynasties, provincial graduates (juren) who passed the metropolitan examination became tribute scholars (gongshi), and those who then succeeded in the palace examination became presented scholars (jinshi). In the palace examination the top three candidates were, in order, the zhuangyuan (top scholar), the bangyan (second), and the tanhua (third). The Ming held 89 examination sessions and produced 24,536 jinshi; the Qing held 112 sessions and produced about 26,000 jinshi.

In 1905 the examination was abolished by the Empress Dowager Cixi, after a history spanning more than 1,300 years. To remember it, recall that it began in the Sui, flourished in the Tang, ended in the Qing, and produced the zhuangyuan, bangyan, and tanhua.

Tang-dynasty guqin are the earliest reliably dated instruments among surviving zithers, and rare treasures within China's guqin-making tradition. 'The Tang is round' (Tang yuan) is an old saying about guqin form that has come down to our own day.

blocks.caption: Tang-Dynasty Guqin and the Saying 'The Tang Is Round'

blocks.text: Guqin making advanced enormously in the Tang. The 'Jiuxiao Huanpei' and 'Dasheng Yiyin' zithers made for the Tang imperial family by the Lei family of Sichuan are celebrated surviving instruments, and Tang zithers have been prized in every age as rare treasures. Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated are those made in the Tang, and nearly twenty Tang instruments survive today.

On the matter of guqin form, the ancients spoke of 'the Tang is round'. Roundness is indeed one feature of Tang zithers, but the saying is not exact - not every round-bodied zither is a Tang instrument. The Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi', one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum, belongs to this group of surviving Tang zithers.

When you look at a Tang zither in the gallery, first take in its rounded outline, crackle patterns and name, then weigh the precision behind the old saying 'the Tang is round' - roundness is one feature of Tang instruments, but not the only criterion.

blocks.text: The Yue kiln was a porcelain kiln of Shaoxing's Yue Prefecture in Zhejiang during the Tang and Five Dynasties periods, with its main kiln sites spread around Shanglin Lake in Cixi. As Shaoxing was called 'Yue Prefecture' under the Sui and Tang dynasties, the kiln took the name 'Yue'.

blocks.caption: The Yue Kiln and Secret-Colour Celadon

blocks.text: In his Classic of Tea, the Tang writer Lu Yu wrote: 'For bowls, Yue Prefecture is the finest. Its porcelain resembles jade and ice.' In the late Tang and Five Dynasties, the finest Yue kiln celadon, with its green of 'a thousand peaks', was reserved exclusively as tribute for the court; commoners were not permitted to use it, which is why it was called 'secret colour' (mise).

On 3 April 1987, the underground palace of the Famen Temple pagoda was opened, yielding thirteen pieces of secret-colour porcelain, now kept at the Famen Temple Museum. In the late Northern Song, as ceramic techniques coarsened, the Yue kiln declined; in the mid Southern Song, it ceased production altogether.

As you look at Yue celadon, weigh the phrase 'like jade, like ice' against the body of a piece, then consider the kiln's rise and fall from the golden age of the Tang to the Song - the very source of Chinese celadon laid out before you in the cases.
