blocks.text: In 2012, the Hong Kong industrialist Mr. Cao Qiyong, a noted native of Zhejiang, and his wife donated 160 pieces (groups) of lacquerware they had treasured for years to the Zhejiang Museum. Spanning from the Song to the Qing dynasties, this collection is an important source of the museum's lacquer holdings.

blocks.caption: The Lacquerware Donated by Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong

blocks.text: Appraisal found that the donated lacquerware includes 21 first-grade artefacts, 118 second-grade and 15 third-grade. Among them, the carved red-lacquer (tihong) plate of children at play by the Yuan master carver Zhang Cheng is a national-treasure-grade work, one of only four known pieces bearing the mark 'made by Zhang Cheng'.

In January 2012, Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong donated 160 pieces of lacquerware from the Song to the Qing dynasties to the museum. In the displays at the Zhijiang Campus, this lacquerware, together with bronzes, ceramics and more, reveals another dimension of Zhejiang's craftsmanship.

As you look at this lacquerware, note techniques like tihong (carved red lacquer), where layer after layer of lacquer is applied and then carved, and appreciate how, from Song to Qing, a single lacquer piece took shape through dozens of processes and the accumulation of time.

741fd9f5-cbb5-5a29-966d-750cfd5d2d6a.name: The Lacquerware Donated by Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong

blocks.text: The ivory carving of twin birds facing the sun is a masterpiece of line engraving from the Hemudu culture and one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. It was made by the Hemudu people of the Neolithic age, some 6,000 to 7,000 years ago.

blocks.caption: Ivory Carving of Twin Birds Facing the Sun

blocks.text: The carving is 16.6 cm long, 5.9 cm across at its widest surviving point and 1.2 cm thick. At its centre, five concentric circles form a sun motif, encircled by a ring of flame patterns, while on either side two birds with hooked beaks look up and face each other. It is the finest example of the line-engraving craft of the Hemudu site.
Among the same group of Hemudu ivory objects there are works best known for the 'double fire bird' motif, showing that birds and the sun were themes the Hemudu people returned to again and again.

When you come upon this carving in the gallery, first look at the concentric-circle sun at its centre, then the two birds gazing up at each other on either side - an imagining of light and birds from seven thousand years ago, preserved to this day through a few engraved lines.

7761fd8c-06f2-5e4a-8343-5144175672c2.name: Ivory Carving of Twin Birds Facing the Sun

blocks.text: The Yuan Longquan kiln boat-shaped water dropper is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. It is a celadon scholar's object of the Longquan kiln family - a small vessel used in the study to hold water for grinding ink.

blocks.caption: The Yuan Longquan Kiln Boat-Shaped Water Dropper

blocks.text: The Longquan kiln flourished in the Southern Song, when improved glaze recipes produced shades such as powder blue and plum green. Fashioned in the shape of a little boat, this water dropper is a fine example of the scholar's objects of Longquan celadon - practical, and full of the elegant charm of the literati study.

After passing the large Longquan dishes and bowls in the ceramics gallery, encountering this little boat that fits in the palm makes you appreciate that the Longquan kiln produced not only grand wares but also something so delicate and light.

As you look at it, reflect: though the water dropper is tiny, it must both store water and release it drop by drop - a piece of celadon that fuses the beauty of an object with the daily act of writing.

7a93901c-1ccc-51e6-ae5e-392a22bc1abe.name: The Yuan Longquan Kiln Boat-Shaped Water Dropper

blocks.text: The Han dynasty (202 BC–9 AD, 25–220 AD) was the second unified imperial dynasty in Chinese history, divided into the Western Han (202 BC–9 AD) and the Eastern Han (25–220 AD). Together the two Han saw 29 emperors over 406 years. The first emperor of the Western Han was Gaozu (Liu Bang), and the first of the Eastern Han was Emperor Guangwu (Liu Xiu).

Liu Bang ascended the throne in 202 BC and named his state 'Han'. Early in the dynasty, to pacify various regional powers, he pursued a parallel system in which commandery-county administration and enfeoffed kingdoms coexisted. Emperors Wen and Jing governed by the Huang-Lao principles of light levies and thrift, remembered as the 'Rule of Wen and Jing'. Emperor Wu reigned for 54 years and twice sent Zhang Qian on missions to the Western Regions; the Silk Road took shape in the late Western Han.

In 9 AD Wang Mang formally usurped the throne and proclaimed the Xin dynasty, ending the Western Han. In 25 AD Liu Xiu, a scion of the Han house, declared himself emperor south of Hao county — Emperor Guangwu — and reunified the realm by 37 AD. Because Luoyang lay east of the old capital Chang'an, later historians called his dynasty the Eastern Han.

In 184 the Yellow Turban rebellion led by Zhang Jiao broke out, and in 220 Cao Pi, son of Cao Cao, replaced the Han, formally opening the Three Kingdoms era. To remember the Han, hold onto these nodes: the Rule of Wen and Jing, Emperor Wu's territorial expansion, Guangwu's restoration, and the Han's end at the hands of Cao Pi.

Some of China's most important artefacts are placed by the state on a national list barring them from overseas exhibition. They may only be shown within China and may not be lent abroad for touring shows. Five groups of artefacts at the Zhejiang Museum are on this list.

On 18 January 2002, the State Administration of Cultural Heritage issued the First Catalogue of Artefacts Barred from Overseas Exhibition, listing 64 objects, of which three were held by the Zhejiang Museum, including the King Jade Cong unearthed at Liangzhu, kept by the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology. In the Third Catalogue, announced on 19 August 2013, two more artefacts from the Zhejiang Museum were included.

All five groups of artefacts are displayed in the exhibition 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture' at the Zhijiang Campus. In other words, walk the full length of this exhibition and you will see all five national treasures barred from overseas exhibition in one go.
Take 'barred from overseas exhibition' as an important hint as you look around: anything on this list is a core artefact deserving special protection and especially careful viewing.

7f3f6526-7e2a-5d1e-a8bd-a68fcc2ce405.name: Lingering Snow on the Broken Bridge

blocks.text: Longquan celadon was a system of kilns centred on the ancient kiln sites of Longquan city in Zhejiang, with branches spread widely across the surrounding region. The Longquan kiln is generally held to have reached its golden age in the Southern Song.

blocks.caption: The Longquan Kiln and Its Powder-Blue and Plum-Green Glazes

blocks.text: By improving glaze recipes, the Longquan kiln created unprecedented shades such as powder blue (fencing) and plum green (meizi qing), admired by collectors through the ages and earning the kiln a place among the famous kilns of the Song dynasty. Glazes fell into two types, lime glazes and lime-alkali glazes. The Northern Song used lime glazes; the Southern Song used lime-alkali glazes, which could be applied in multiple coats to build up a thick glaze layer - the powder-blue glaze is of this lime-alkali type.

Firing temperatures at the Longquan kiln ranged from 1,180 to 1,230 C; plum green required the highest heat, 1,250 to 1,280 C. In September 2009, the traditional firing techniques of Longquan celadon were inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Compare the powder-blue and plum-green glazes side by side, and gesture how thick the glaze feels, and you will understand how Southern Song craftsmen used lime-alkali glaze to render green as warm and smooth as jade.

7f792a90-7796-57ed-bc27-e69b3fe33fbc.name: The Longquan Kiln and Its Powder-Blue and Plum-Green Glazes

blocks.text: Yue Fei (1103–1142), courtesy name Pengju, was a native of Tangyin in Xiangzhou and the celebrated Southern Song general who resisted the Jin. From the time he served under Zong Ze in the second year of Jianyan (1128) until 1141 (the eleventh year of Shaoxing), he led the Yue Family Army through hundreds of engagements, large and small, against the Jin forces.

In 1140 (the tenth year of Shaoxing), Wanyan Wuzhu, fourth son of the Jin founder, broke the peace treaty and attacked the Song. Yue Fei struck north, recovering Zhengzhou and other places, then routed the Jin at Yancheng and Yingchang and advanced on Zhuxian Town. The Yue Family Army was famed for refusing to dismantle houses even when freezing and refusing to plunder even when starving; even the opposing Jurchens marveled that it was easier to move a mountain than to move the Yue Family Army.

Emperor Gaozong, set on peace, ordered a withdrawal with twelve gilt tablets of command, and Yue Fei was compelled to turn his army back. On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month in the eleventh year of Shaoxing (January 27, 1142), the eve of the new year, Yue Fei was executed at the Fengbo Pavilion of the court of judicial review in Hangzhou on trumped-up charges; his eldest son Yue Yun and his general Zhang Xian were put to death as well.

After Emperor Xiaozong came to the throne he rehabilitated Yue Fei, granting him the posthumous title Wumu in 1178 (the fifth year of Chunxi), and in 1204 (the fourth year of Jiatai) Emperor Ningzong posthumously created him Prince of E. To remember Yue Fei, recall the Yue Family Army, the drive on Zhuxian Town, the twelve gilt tablets, and the injustice of Fengbo Pavilion.

85ea281c-8741-505e-a7f0-62400f5b33ba.name: Lingyin Temple and Its Zen Grove

blocks.text: The Northern and Southern Dynasties period (420–589) runs from the Liu Song's replacement of the Jin in 420 to the Sui's conquest of Chen in 589. The Southern Dynasties comprised the Liu Song, Southern Qi, Liang, and Chen, all with capitals at Jiankang; the Northern Dynasties comprised the Northern Wei, Eastern Wei, Western Wei, Northern Qi, and Northern Zhou.

The Northern Wei was founded by the Xianbei clan of Tuoba. In 439 Emperor Taiwu conquered the Northern Liang, ending the Sixteen Kingdoms period and confronting the Liu Song of the south. Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang in 493 and carried out a sinicization program, changing the Tuoba surname to Yuan and intermarrying with the great Chinese clans.

In 523, at the end of the Northern Wei, the Rebellion of the Six Garrisons broke out, and in 534 the state split into the Eastern Wei and the Western Wei; the Northern Qi and Northern Zhou then rose in succession. In 550 the Western Wei and Northern Zhou created the fubing garrison-soldier system, and the Northern Zhou instituted six ministries after the Rites of Zhou — the origins of the Sui and Tang institutional framework.

In 581 Yang Jian replaced the Northern Zhou with the Sui, and in 589 the Sui conquered Chen, ending a division of China that had lasted 280 years since the Yongjia catastrophe. To remember this period, recall the four Southern dynasties all centered on Jiankang, the five Northern dynasties, and the Sui's reunification.

Wu Changshuo (12 September 1844 - 29 November 1927) came from Zhangwu village, Anji County, Huzhou, Zhejiang. A seal carver active in the late Qing and early Republic, he was also accomplished in calligraphy and painting.

blocks.caption: Wu Changshuo and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: In 1904, Wu Changshuo became director of the Xiling Seal Art Society on Gushan, Hangzhou, calling himself the 'seal-craving beggar of the five lakes'. He once said he began learning to write poetry at thirty and did not take up painting until fifty. In his later years he settled in Shanghai and was later grouped with the 'Shanghai School' (Haipai). His works include the Collected Poems of Foulu, the Collected Seals of Foulu and the Album of Paintings by Wu Changshuo.
In December 1957, Wu Changshuo's family donated artefacts to the Zhejiang Museum, making his works part of the museum's painting and calligraphy collection.

As you look at the museum's paintings, calligraphy and seals, set Wu Changshuo's works beside his remark about 'taking up painting at fifty' - late blooming yet tireless, exactly the shared temperament of the Shanghai School and the painting-and-calligraphy tradition of Zhejiang.

88e71f5d-0fd2-5907-a3ed-a4bb4aed0e90.name: Wu Changshuo and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: The Liangzhu Museum stands in Meilizhou Park, Liangzhu Subdistrict, Yuhang District, Hangzhou, Zhejiang. It is a museum devoted to displaying and studying the Liangzhu culture, and its predecessor, the Liangzhu Culture Museum, opened in 1994.

The new building was begun in March 2005 and opened to the public in October 2008. Designed by the British architect David Chipperfield, its concept is 'a handful of jade cones scattered across the ground', realized as four elongated volumes that are not quite parallel. The museum covers about 40,000 square metres, with a floor area of about 10,000 square metres and more than 4,000 square metres of exhibition space, comprising three permanent galleries, one temporary gallery and a collection store.

The permanent exhibition, under the overall theme 'The Liangzhu Culture: Proof of Five Thousand Years of Chinese Civilization', is divided into three parts — 'Discovery and the Pursuit of Truth', 'The Ancient Liangzhu State' and 'Liangzhu Civilization' — and displays more than 1,000 treasured objects including Liangzhu jades, pottery and lacquerware. In 2009 the exhibition won the top award among China's Top Ten Museum Exhibitions. In August 2017 the museum upgraded the permanent exhibition in light of the latest archaeological findings, reopening in June 2018.

Follow the order 'Discovery — the Ancient State — Civilization'; the three sections correspond exactly to 'archaeological discovery, reconstruction of the ancient state, and the value of the civilization' — the smoothest route for reading the exhibition.

891c98ae-bf30-5e71-ade3-03555e4c56ab.name: How the Ten Scenes of West Lake Are Viewed

blocks.text: The Mojiaoshan site is the centre of the Liangzhu culture: 670 metres east–west and 450 metres north–south, covering more than 300,000 square metres with a relative height of about 8 metres. The entire Liangzhu site cluster is distributed around it, and it can be considered the centre of political power.

blocks.caption: Mojiaoshan: The Power Centre of Liangzhu

blocks.text: The Mojiaoshan terrace is rectangular and trapezoidal in profile, 9 to 15 metres high, and entirely artificial. To build a platform of 300,000 square metres would have required an estimated 500,000 cubic metres of earth and at least 600,000 person-days of labour. If completed in 100 days, that means 6,000 people working continuously, and with organizers and provisioning personnel, about 10,000 people in total.

Yan Wenming suggested that Mojiaoshan may have been the capital of a state. On the terrace, rammed-earth foundations covering more than 1,400 square metres and postholes have been found, and within a 34-square-kilometre area around it at least fifty sites of various sizes cluster densely.

When you climb onto the Mojiaoshan terrace in the Liangzhu Archaeological Site Park, first take in the extent of the platform, then compare it with the small sites surrounding it — you will understand why this terrace, built by the labour of some 10,000 people, is called the power centre of Liangzhu.

893ee811-737d-54ca-a22a-d3a1fce35880.name: Mojiaoshan: The Power Centre of Liangzhu

blocks.text: The Ming dynasty (1368–1644) was the unified dynasty that followed the Yuan and the last unified dynasty founded by the Han Chinese, spanning 12 reigns and 16 emperors over 276 years. In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed himself emperor at Yingtian Prefecture (present-day Nanjing) as Ming Taizu, adopting the dynastic title Great Ming.

In the thirteenth year of Hongwu (1380), Taizu executed his chancellor on charges of seizing power and building a faction, using the occasion to abolish both the chancellorship and the Secretariat, concentrating power in the emperor. Prince Yan, Zhu Di, seized the throne through the Jingnan campaign, becoming Emperor Chengzu; in the eighteenth year of Yongle (1420) he moved the capital to Shuntian Prefecture (present-day Beijing).

Emperor Chengzu sent Zheng He on his voyages to the Western Ocean seven times, reaching as far as the Somalia region of East Africa, and commissioned the great encyclopedia the Yongle Dadian. In 1449 the Tumu Crisis saw Emperor Yingzong captured by the Oirat forces. As grand secretary, Zhang Juzheng created the assessment-of-performance law and, in the ninth year of Wanli (1581), carried out the Single Whip tax reform.

In the seventeenth year of Chongzhen (1644), Li Zicheng established the Dashun state and took Beijing; the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself on Coal Hill, and the Ming fell. To remember the Ming, recall Taizu's abolition of the chancellorship, the Yongle emperor's move of the capital, Zheng He's voyages, and the Single Whip tax reform.

89a21706-5676-56aa-ab3c-6ab2b48991d8.name: Su Shi and the Governing of West Lake

8ddba328-608b-57b4-81bb-f383b22c1310.name: Moonlight and Reflections on West Lake

9144e185-d474-5c5d-a39b-0ab00af80c0d.name: The 1985 New Ten Scenes of West Lake

blocks.text: The Gushan Campus is the oldest campus of the Zhejiang Museum, set at the southern foot of Solitary Hill (Gushan) by West Lake in Hangzhou. It adjoins the Bai Causeway and the 'Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake' scenic spot to the east and the Xiling Seal Art Society to the west. Completed in the autumn of 1993 and covering 20,400 square metres, its buildings form a layout described as 'a museum in a garden, a garden in a museum'.

blocks.caption: The Gushan Campus and 'A Museum in a Garden, a Garden in a Museum'

blocks.text: The campus also includes the Zhejiang West Lake Art Museum and the Wenglan Pavilion. The Wenglan Pavilion stands on the west side of the campus. Built in 1783 (the 48th year of the Qianlong reign), it was one of the seven imperial pavilions holding copies of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (Siku Quanshu) in the Qing dynasty. Destroyed by fire in 1861 (the 11th year of the Xianfeng reign) and rebuilt in 1880 (the 6th year of the Guangxu reign), it is the only survivor of the three southern pavilions. In 2001 the State Council designated it a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level; in 2006 it underwent the largest restoration since the founding of the People's Republic, and it reopened to the public in June 2013.

The main building, completed on 29 September 1993, and the pre-existing gardens of Gushan together make up this 'museum within a garden'. Use the phrase 'a museum in a garden, a garden in a museum' as your route: first take in the ceramics and calligraphy and paintings in the main hall, then walk to the Wenglan Pavilion and feel how the museum's boundary almost dissolves into the landscape of West Lake.

Most new exhibitions have now moved to the Zhijiang Campus, but Gushan remains the spiritual home of the museum. If you want to understand how a museum can live in harmony with a lake and its hills, the Gushan Campus is the most direct answer.

917dfb28-49c6-5a13-975c-0901a3248fc5.name: The Gushan Campus and 'A Museum in a Garden, a Garden in a Museum'

blocks.text: The Twenty-Four Histories is the collective name for the twenty-four official histories compiled by the successive Chinese dynasties. Regarded as orthodox by every ruling house, they are also known as the 'Standard Histories'. They cover more than four thousand years of Chinese history, from the legendary Yellow Emperor to the seventeenth year of the Ming Chongzhen era (1644), in 3,213 volumes, all written in the annals-and-biographies format of basic annals and biographies.

The term 'Standard History' first appears in the Bibliographic Treatise of the Book of Sui; after the Qianlong emperor officially designated the Twenty-Four Histories, the name became exclusive to them. Once the Records of the Three Kingdoms was completed, it joined the Records of the Grand Historian, the Book of Han, and the Book of the Later Han as the 'Former Four Histories'.

When the History of Ming was completed in the Yongzheng era of the Qing, the collection became the Twenty-Two Histories; the addition of the Old Book of Tang made twenty-three. While compiling the Four Treasuries, the Old History of the Five Dynasties, recovered from the Yongle Dadian, was added to make the Twenty-Four Histories. In 1921 the New History of Yuan was added, making the Twenty-Five Histories.
To remember the Twenty-Four Histories, recall the annals-and-biographies format, the Former Four Histories, and the Qianlong emperor's selection of twenty-four official histories.

The Zhejiang Museum holds more than one hundred thousand artefacts that span virtually every period of Zhejiang's history, a comprehensive regional collection built up through local archaeology and donations.

blocks.caption: A Collection of Over One Hundred Thousand Objects and Its System

blocks.text: Highlights of the collection include Hemudu culture pottery, lacquerware, woodwork and ivory artefacts; Liangzhu culture jades and silk; the swords of the Yue kings; celadon from the Yue kiln, the Longquan kiln and the Southern Song Guan (imperial) kiln; mirrors from Kuaiji and Huzhou; works by renowned painters and calligraphers such as Wu Changshuo, Huang Binhong and Sha Menghai; and the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains by the Yuan-dynasty painter Huang Gongwang.

The collection has also grown through donations: on 22 March 1955, Huang Binhong's family donated artefacts including 1,848 titles of books, 2,416 letters, 810 manuscripts, 10 genealogies, 65 records of painting appraisal at the Palace Museum and 6 volumes of decipherings of ancient seals; in December 1957, Wu Changshuo's family donated artefacts; in May 1991 the 'Ma Dingxiang Chinese Numismatics Research Center' was established; and in January 2012, Mr. and Mrs. Cao Qiyong donated 160 pieces of lacquerware from the Song to the Qing dynasties.

Faced with more than one hundred thousand objects, you need not see every one. The most efficient way to visit is to follow the two threads of the 'top treasures of the museum' and the 'artefacts barred from overseas exhibition', then choose one category that matches your interest and look deeper.

9600a3eb-78a4-5bd0-bb33-fc2578bb724b.name: Yanggong Causeway and the Ming Dredging

blocks.text: The bone plough is a bone digging tool for turning soil unearthed at the Hemudu site. It was the Hemudu people's trusty implement for tilling the land and planting rice, and it is the emblematic artefact of what is called 'plough-till agriculture'.

The two formal excavations at the Hemudu site yielded about two hundred bone ploughs. Of the 4,670 artefacts recovered in the second formal excavation, bone objects made up 48.6 per cent - a measure of how much bone implements weighed in the Hemudu remains.

Professor You Xiuling of Zhejiang Agricultural University proposed that the bone plough was the tool with which the Hemudu people turned the soil, and he named the farming form of the time 'plough-till agriculture' after it - a view now widely accepted in scholarship. The site also yielded vast quantities of cultivated rice in deposits 40 to 50 cm thick, a sensation in academic circles.

As you look at the bone plough, think of it together with the layer upon layer of cultivated rice: it was with bone tools like this that the Hemudu people turned the soil and planted rice, and thereby took root in the watery landscape of Hangzhou Bay six or seven thousand years ago.

The Qin dynasty (221–207 BC) was the first unified, centrally governed empire in Chinese history, whose royal house bore the Ying surname. From 230 to 221 BC, King Zheng of Qin successively conquered the six other major states, unifying the Central Plains and styling himself 'First Emperor', from which point China had the title of emperor.

The Qin established a centralized system built on the imperial institution, the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers, and the commandery-county system, and standardized the currency (the Qin ban liang coin) and weights and measures. Li Si revised the Qin variant of the ancient seal script to create small seal script, which was adopted throughout the realm, while Cheng Miao further simplified it into clerical script. Its military system was notable for the twenty-rank nobility order devised by Shang Yang, and the Qin people were called 'the state that prizes merit in battle'.

In 214 BC the First Emperor ordered Meng Tian to lead an army of 300,000 against the Xiongnu in the north, and to join the old walls of Qin, Zhao, and Yan into a line stretching ten thousand li from Lintao to Liaodong, hence the name 'the Great Wall of Ten Thousand Li'. The First Emperor undertook large-scale construction of palaces, mausoleums, roads, and the Great Wall, and the terracotta warriors have been inscribed on the World Heritage List.

The 'burning of books' took place in 213 BC, followed a year later by the 'burying of scholars'. In 209 BC Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rose in revolt at Dazexiang, and in 207 BC Ziying, the king of Qin, surrendered to Liu Bang; the Qin fell three years after the First Emperor's death. To remember the Qin, recall 'the first great unification, the imperial institution, the commandery-county system, and the Great Wall of Ten Thousand Li'.

Founded in November 1929, the Zhejiang Museum is one of the earliest regional comprehensive museums in China. It was once known as the 'Zhejiang West Lake Museum' and the 'Provincial West Lake Museum'. Its beginnings lie right by West Lake, closely tied to the legacy of the modern West Lake Exposition.

blocks.caption: The History of the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: After the West Lake Exposition closed in November 1929, the Zhejiang provincial government set up the Zhejiang West Lake Museum at the southern foot of Solitary Hill (Gushan), using the Wenglan Pavilion, the Wang Yangming Shrine, the Shengyin Arhat Hall and the Taiyi Fenqing Studio to preserve the exposition's relics, with Chen Qihuai appointed director. In February 1930 it was renamed the 'Provincial West Lake Museum'. In May 1949 it was taken over by the People's Liberation Army entering Hangzhou. On 29 September 1993 the new building was completed, covering 2.04 hectares with a total floor area of 7,360 square metres, built at a cost of 20 million yuan.

Since then it has remained at the forefront of Chinese museums: on 1 January 2004 it became the first provincial museum in the country to open free of charge year-round; in 2008 it was rated among the first batch of 'National First-Class Museums'; and in 2009 it was designated a 'Nationally and Locally Co-Built National Museum' by the State Administration of Cultural Heritage and the Ministry of Finance. In December that year, the Wulin campus was completed and opened.

Keep this history in mind as you explore: the milestones from 1929 to 2004 - Chen Qihuai, the Solitary Hill buildings and free admission - together trace a thread running through a century of cultural life around West Lake.

9d5f30ce-f7b7-5897-b564-e02a11a0fea7.name: The History of the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, when the moon is believed to be at its fullest. Its core meaning is reunion: families gather, share round mooncakes, and admire the full moon together.
Moon-viewing became an established custom in the Tang and Song dynasties. Many Chinese scenic names, such as Three Pools Mirroring the Moon, were designed precisely for this night.

a0a3e522-99bb-518b-9630-1d3e3f9dae16.name: Bai Juyi and the Bai Causeway Tradition

blocks.text: The Silk Road was the overland route leading from the ancient Han and Tang capitals of Chang'an or Luoyang, through Gansu and Xinjiang, to Central Asia, West Asia, and Europe, and linking the lands around the Mediterranean. It takes its name from silk, the most influential of the goods carried westward along it. The term 'Silk Road' first appeared in an atlas published in 1877 by the German geographer Baron Ferdinand von Richthofen.

In the second year of Jianyuan (139 BC), Zhang Qian set out from Chang'an with more than a hundred attendants on a mission to the Western Regions; captured by the Xiongnu along the way, he finally returned to Chang'an in 126 BC after many hardships. Historians praise his first western journey as having 'opened a road through the void'. In the second year of Shenjue (60 BC) under Emperor Xuan, the Protectorate of the Western Regions was established, and in the Eastern Han, Ban Chao again traveled to the Western Regions, reopening the long-abandoned Silk Road.

The traditional Silk Road is divided into eastern, central, and western sections: the eastern section runs from Chang'an or Luoyang to the Yumen and Yangguan passes, the central section from beyond those passes to the Pamir mountains, and the western section from the Pamirs westward through Central and West Asia to Europe. In the Battle of Talas in 751, Chinese papermaking spread to the Islamic world through craftsmen taken prisoner.

On June 22, 2014, the Silk Road, together with the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site. To remember the Silk Road, recall Zhang Qian's pioneering journeys, Ban Chao's reopening of the route, and the origin of its name in silk.

The commonly accepted dates for the Liangzhu culture are c. 5300 to 4000 years ago; in calibrated terms, the sites date from c. 3300 to 2000 BC. Museum labels and publications mostly follow this main chronology.

blocks.caption: The Chronology and Periods of Liangzhu

blocks.text: Scholars do not fully agree on the dates. Shao Wangping placed Liangzhu at c. 5300–4000 years ago or slightly earlier, a span of more than 1,200 years; Cho-yun Hsu placed it at c. 5300–4700 years ago, lasting about 600 years; and Hayashi Minao held that it flourished c. 6000–5000 years ago.

After Liangzhu, the Maqiao culture shows a marked decline in agriculture, jade and settlement. The beast-mask motif of Liangzhu jade shares many features with the taotie motif of Shang bronzes: Li Xueqin believed the relationship was close though not a direct descent, while Hayashi Minao held that the taotie of the Shang–Zhou period derived from the Liangzhu beast-mask motif.

You needn't dwell on the exact numbers. Just remember the round figure of '5300 to 4000 years ago', and note that Liangzhu is earlier than the Shang dynasty but later than Hemudu — that is enough to place it in time.

a0d2ece0-3148-51b3-992a-bc0f60391cf2.name: The Chronology and Periods of Liangzhu

blocks.text: Rice agriculture was the economic foundation of the Liangzhu culture. The Liangzhu people skillfully cultivated with stone plows, and rice began to become the staple food, making Liangzhu a major representative of prehistoric rice-growing civilization in China.

Economically, Liangzhu developed intensive rice agriculture. New tools appeared, such as triangular stone plows and soil breakers, and plow cultivation replaced hoeing with the spade. Archaeologists have also found a tool called the qianbu, used to drain water into paddy fields, mix the mud and level the field soil. Domesticated animals, including pigs, also appear in Liangzhu culture.

The World Heritage Committee described Liangzhu as an early regional state 'founded on rice agriculture'. Some scholars have proposed agricultural decline as one explanation for the end of the Liangzhu culture. An economy capable of sustaining large-scale intensive farming while managing water and flood control was precisely the foundation of Liangzhu's complex society.

In the exhibition, read the group of farm tools — the stone plow, the soil breaker and the qianbu — alongside the city walls and the water system. Then you will see that Liangzhu's jade power and royal authority were in fact built upon wide paddy fields.

Liangzhu pottery is famed for its burnished black ware, which immediately evokes parallels with the Longshan culture of Shandong. This was also the class of finds that first drew attention to Liangzhu archaeology.

Liangzhu pottery is chiefly grey-black ware, complemented by grit-tempered red ware. Ring feet and flat bases are common, and the wares were made on the fast wheel. Forms include pots, jars, stemmed dishes and basins, with burnished black ware being the most striking.

Liangzhu remains were first discovered in the 1930s and were recognized by their burnished black pottery, at the time called 'Longshan culture of the Hangzhou Bay area' or 'Zhejiang Longshan culture'. Black pottery was one of the key traits by which Liangzhu was first identified.

When you view Liangzhu pottery, first note the burnished black ware and the fast-wheel forms, then check the ring feet and flat bases. A piece of grey-black pottery often tells you more about the everyday craftsmanship of the Liangzhu people than the jades do.

Shili hongzhuang ('a ten-li red trousseau') is a marriage custom of eastern Zhejiang, centred on Ninghai County. It takes its name from the practice in which a daughter's dowry - from beds and furniture down to needles, thread and headdresses - was so complete that the procession bearing it stretched for ten li (roughly five kilometres). The custom began in the Southern Song and flourished in the Ming and Qing dynasties.

blocks.caption: Shili Hongzhuang and the Marriage Customs of Ningbo and Shaoxing

blocks.text: In 2008, the shili hongzhuang wedding custom was inscribed on China's national intangible cultural heritage list. The local Ninghai crafts of vermilion-and-gold woodcarving (zhujin mudiao) and gold-ground painted lacquer (nijin caiqi) provided the technical support for making these exquisite dowries. Ninghai dowries centre on vermilion-and-gold woodcarving and mainly include bridal sedan chairs, wedding beds, carrying cases, vessels and various ornaments, giving rise to the saying of the 'thousand-work bed and ten-thousand-work sedan chair'.

According to legend, in the late Northern Song, the Prince of Kang, Zhao Gou, fleeing pursuit by the Jin army in eastern Zhejiang, was rescued by a country girl. After he took the throne as Emperor Gaozong, he decreed that all women of eastern Zhejiang might be granted royal honours and ride in dragon-and-phoenix bridal sedan chairs on their wedding day. During the Cultural Revolution, shili hongzhuang objects were badly damaged as 'the four olds'. In the early reform era, many Westerners rushed to Ninghai to buy them up, and artefacts were lost on a serious scale; the Ninghai antique dealer He Xiaodao began to collect shili hongzhuang artefacts, and in 2003 the Shili Hongzhuang Museum opened.

When you see the wedding beds, sedan chairs and vessels of shili hongzhuang at the Zhejiang Museum, picture them as a trousseau procession on the move: from Ninghai to Hangzhou, vermilion-and-gold woodcarving and gold-ground painted lacquer carried the joy of marriage and the skill of the craftsmen right into the museum.

blocks.text: The age of Liangzhu was not home to a single culture. In northern China and along the Yangtze, cultures such as Hongshan and Lingjiatan were active at the same time, together forming the 'star-filled sky' of the origins of Chinese civilization.

blocks.caption: The Stars of Chinese Civilization in Liangzhu's Time

blocks.text: The Hongshan culture is a predominantly agricultural Neolithic culture of northern China, dated c. 4700–2900 BC. Its jade dragon is hailed as 'China's first dragon' and is prohibited from travelling abroad for exhibition. The Lingjiatan culture spread across the Chaohu Lake area of the middle and lower Yangtze; some 5,000 years ago the Lingjiatan site was a large late Neolithic settlement, where an altar and a large clan cemetery have been found.

These cultures share much in jade, altars and sacred authority — the Hongshan jade dragon, the Lingjiatan jades and the Liangzhu cong all remind us that 'Chinese civilization' was jointly born of many regions influencing one another.
Look beyond Liangzhu — turn your gaze to the Hongshan jade dragon and the Lingjiatan altar. Liangzhu is the brightest beam in this starry sky, but far from the only one.

blocks.text: Qin Shi Huang (259–210 BC), surnamed Ying and named Zheng, was born at Handan, the capital of Zhao, the son of King Zhuangxiang of Qin and Queen Zhao Ji. He came to the throne at thirteen, conquered the six states and founded the Qin at thirty-nine, and styled himself the First Emperor — the first ruler in Chinese history to bear the imperial title. The Ming thinker Li Zhi hailed him as 'the one emperor for a thousand ages'.

Between 230 and 221 BC, King Zheng of Qin conquered in turn the six states of Han, Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan, and Qi, unifying the realm. After unification, the First Emperor carried forward the commandery-county system and centralization introduced by Shang Yang's reforms, standardized weights and measures, and imposed common axle widths for carts, a common script, shared standards of conduct, and a unified legal code.

During his reign the First Emperor undertook many great projects — the Great Wall, the Epang Palace, and his mausoleum at Mount Li among them — imposing such heavy corvée labor on the people that it became a principal reason the Qin collapsed a mere three years after his death.

To remember Qin Shi Huang, recall the 'emperor for a thousand ages', the unified script and standard axle gauge, the commandery-county system, and the building of the Wall and the mausoleum — and also the other face of his reign, where grand achievements coexisted with crushing burdens.

The decorated pottery of the Hemudu culture was made by hand by the Hemudu people, with patterns painted or incised on the surface. These pots are important physical evidence for understanding Hemudu life and beliefs. They are thick, grey-black in colour, and often bear cord-marking or motifs of plants and animals.

blocks.caption: Decorated Pottery of the Hemudu Culture

blocks.text: Hemudu pottery was handmade, very thick, grey-black, often polished on the surface, and commonly decorated with cord marks or carved plant and animal designs. The motifs painted on the pottery include birds, fish, rice, the sun, flowers and grasses, with the fish-and-grain basin, the rice-ear basin, the pig-design bowl and the five-leaf motif pottery plaque as representative pieces.

Hemudu pottery reached a considerable standard; the highest estimated firing temperature was 1,000 C. Another account records that pottery from the first phase of the Hemudu site was fired at about 850 C, mainly by the coiling method. The two excavations yielded 1,695 complete or restored vessels, several times that number in sherds, and carbon-tempered black ware predominates among them.

As you look at these decorated pots, first identify the motifs - birds, fish, rice, the sun, flowers and grasses, the watery everyday life the Hemudu people faced day after day - then consider firing temperatures of nearly a thousand degrees (or, by one account, 850 C) to appreciate what kiln-fire it took to shape such a vessel.

ac565d24-9a02-5a99-8acc-cb885f30883d.name: Decorated Pottery of the Hemudu Culture

blocks.text: The Spring and Autumn bronze house of musicians is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. A bronze object on the theme of a house and its musicians, it comes from the Shaoxing area, the heartland of the state of Yue.

blocks.caption: The Spring and Autumn Bronze House of Musicians

blocks.text: According to historical accounts, the bronze house of musicians unearthed at Shaoxing contains figures of a drummer, zither players, a se player and singing performers, recreating a scene of ensemble singing among the Yue people. It freezes a 'little concert' from more than two thousand years ago in bronze.

The state of Yue was one of the principal sources of smelting materials such as copper and tin in the pre-Qin period, and the skill of the Yue people at making swords and blades was a fact universally acknowledged before the Western Han. The bronze house of musicians is a rare work from this deep bronze-casting tradition that depicts a musical scene.

When you look at this little bronze house, first count the musicians and instruments inside, then think of the bronze world of Yue it belongs to - the people of Zhejiang more than two thousand years ago were already combining drums, qin and se in ensemble performance.

b1ddcee4-d6ab-5b03-bdf9-1e51d9e9a842.name: The Spring and Autumn Bronze House of Musicians

blocks.text: Li Dan (born c. 571 BC), honored by posterity as Laozi ('Old Master'), is said to have been born in the village of Qurenli in Li township, Ku county, in the Chu state of the Eastern Zhou, and to have served as a keeper of the archives in the Zhou royal court during the Spring and Autumn period. Laozi is revered as the founder of Daoism and the Taoist religion, and as one of the Three Sages of the East.

The book written in his name, the Laozi, is widely known as the Daodejing and is the classic of Daoism. In the commonly transmitted editions of Heshan Gong of the Han and Wang Bi of the Wei, the work has 81 chapters: the first 37 form the 'Classic of the Way' (Daojing) and the last 42 the 'Classic of Virtue' (Dejing).

Lao Dan advocated ruling through non-action, the unity of heaven and humanity, and quiet non-interference. Along with Zhuang Zhou he is regarded as a leading figure of Daoism, and the two are jointly called 'Lao-Zhuang'. The Records of the Grand Historian records that Confucius once asked Laozi about ritual.

In October 1993, 804 bamboo slips of the Warring States period were unearthed from the Chu tomb at Guodian in Jingmen, Hubei, representing the earliest extant text of the Daodejing. To remember Laozi, recall the Daodejing, rule by non-action, 'Lao-Zhuang', and his role as the founder of Daoism.

Li Shimin (598–649), second son of the Tang founder Li Yuan, was the second emperor of the Tang. On the fourth day of the sixth month in the ninth year of Wude (July 2, 626), Li Shimin ambushed his rivals at the Xuanwu Gate, personally shooting the crown prince Li Jiancheng while Yuchi Jingde killed the Prince of Qi, Li Yuanji — an event known as the Xuanwu Gate Incident. That September the founding emperor abdicated, and Li Shimin took the throne as Emperor Taizong, changing the era name to Zhenguan the following year.

Li Shimin reigned for 23 years (626–649), remembered by posterity as the Zhenguan era. He appointed able men and welcomed frank remonstrance; Wei Zheng bluntly admonished the emperor on more than 200 occasions at court. In the spring of 643, Taizong had portraits of the twenty-four meritorious statesmen painted in the Lingyan Pavilion.

After the Eastern Turkic Khaganate fell in 630, the histories record that the nine clans of the Tiele, the kingdoms of the Western Regions, and Tokhara alike honored him as the 'Heavenly Khan'. In 641 Princess Wencheng of the Tang court married Songtsen Gampo, the tsenpo of Tibet. Emperor Taizong died at the Cuiwei Palace in 649 and was buried at the Zhaoling Mausoleum, with the posthumous title Emperor Wen and temple name Taizong.
To remember Emperor Taizong, recall four things: the Xuanwu Gate Incident, the Zhenguan era, the title Heavenly Khan, and Wei Zheng's frank remonstrance.

The Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi' ('A Colorful Phoenix Sings at Qishan') is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. Made in the Tang dynasty, it is a celebrated surviving guqin and a representative piece in the museum's guqin collection.

blocks.caption: The Tang Seven-Stringed Zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi'

blocks.text: Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated examples are those of the Tang dynasty; nearly twenty Tang zithers have come down to us and have been treasured in every age as rare treasures. 'Cai Feng Ming Qi' belongs precisely to this group of Tang instruments that have survived to this day.

The art of the guqin was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 7 November 2003 and on the first national intangible cultural heritage list on 20 May 2006. This Tang zither is a tangible example of that ancient art that can still be heard today.

When you see this Tang zither, first look at its name and its face, then reflect that it has been silent for nearly fourteen hundred years - an instrument that has carried the aural tradition of the Tang all the way into today's display case.

b78c3e13-f4fd-5626-8150-4744854e50d8.name: The Tang Seven-Stringed Zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi'

blocks.text: Landscape painting, shan shui hua, is the most prestigious genre of Chinese painting. It aims not at topographical accuracy but at scenes the viewer can mentally wander and dwell in.
Maturing in the Song and Yuan dynasties, its vocabulary of mist, distance, and empty space directly shaped real gardens and scenic naming, such as the Ten Scenes of West Lake.
The Northern Song painted clay standing bodhisattva is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum - a polychrome clay sculpture of a bodhisattva from the Song dynasty.

blocks.caption: The Northern Song Painted Clay Standing Bodhisattva

blocks.text: Compared with bronze or porcelain, clay Buddhist images are far harder to preserve; that a painted clay bodhisattva of the Northern Song should survive to this day is remarkable in itself. Like the Buddhist remains of the Five Dynasties Wuyue kingdom, it reminds you, as you look at the sculptures at the Zhejiang Museum, to notice the other path Song sculpture took in materials and form.

bc5f2bd7-6d22-57f2-bf6d-a63c2b7f2272.name: The Northern Song Painted Clay Standing Bodhisattva

blocks.text: The Sui dynasty (581–619) was founded by Emperor Wen (Yang Jian), who received the abdication of the Northern Zhou, and lasted a mere 38 years until Wang Shichong deposed Emperor Gong in 619. In 589 the Sui conquered the Chen of the south, ending the more than 280 years of north-south division that had followed the Yongjia catastrophe of the Western Jin.

Emperor Wen inaugurated the flourishing Kaihuang era, during which the registered population grew from about four million households to over eight million. He abolished the Northern Zhou's six ministries, established the Three Departments and Six Ministries, simplified the state-commandery-county hierarchy to state and county, and instituted the imperial examination system in 587; in 606 Emperor Yang added the jinshi (presented scholar) examination.

In 605 Emperor Yang cut the Tongji Canal and drove forward the construction of the Sui-Tang Grand Canal; he also launched large-scale wars against Goguryeo in 612, 613, and 614. With corvée labor and military service weighing heavily on the people, rebellions broke out across the land.

In 617 Li Yuan raised the standard of revolt at Jinyang (Taiyuan), proclaimed himself emperor and founded the Tang in 618, and the Sui fell in 619. To remember the Sui, recall Emperor Wen's Kaihuang rule, Emperor Yang's canal building and campaigns against Goguryeo, and the dynasty's brief 38-year span.

Calligraphy turns the writing of Chinese characters into an art. Because characters evolved from pictographs and are written with a soft brush, every stroke carries the writer's discipline and temperament.
Inscriptions on tablets, plaques, and seals are everywhere in Chinese landscapes. Seal carving, calligraphy's sister art, is the specialty of Hangzhou's Xiling Seal Art Society.

The former residence of Sha Menghai, master calligrapher and honorary director of the Zhejiang Museum, preserves his works, seals, and everyday objects, linking the museum with modern Chinese calligraphy and the Xiling Seal Art Society.

blocks.text: The Yuan dynasty (1260 or 1271–1368), whose official title was the Great Yuan, was founded by the Mongols in Chinese history and had 11 emperors over 98 years. In 1206 Temüjin was honored as Genghis Khan, founding the Mongol Empire; in 1271 Kublai adopted the Chinese dynastic title Great Yuan and fixed the capital at Dadu (present-day Beijing).

The Yuan was the first unified dynasty in Chinese history to include the word 'Great' in its official title. In 1279 the Yuan conquered the Southern Song, ending the division that had lasted over 520 years since the An Lushan Rebellion of the Tang. Kublai adopted Chinese administrative practices, establishing the Secretariat, the Bureau of Military Affairs, and the Censorate, in a political structure that blended Mongol and Chinese elements.

The Yuan set up provincial secretariats and the Commission for Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs, among other institutions. Drama and performing arts aimed at commoners flourished, most notably Yuan opera (yuanqu); in 1312 Emperor Renzong restored the imperial examinations with Cheng-Zhu Neo-Confucianism as the subject matter, a revival known as the Yanyou examinations.

In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming and sent Xu Da on a northern campaign that captured Dadu; the Yuan's rule over China ended, and the Yuan court retreated to the Mongolian steppe, remembered as the Northern Yuan. To remember the Yuan, recall its Mongol founders, the title Great Yuan, the provincial system, and Yuan opera.

The Opium Wars were two conflicts between the Qing empire and the Western powers in the mid-19th century; because the first was sparked by the prohibition of opium and the second is regarded as its continuation, the two are jointly called the Opium Wars. The First Opium War was launched by Britain against China in 1840 and ended with the Treaty of Nanking in 1842.

In 1839 Lin Zexu ordered the confiscation of all opium in Guangzhou; Charles Elliot, the British superintendent of trade in China, handed over 20,000 chests (1,300 tons) of opium, which Lin Zexu destroyed at Humen. The Treaty of Nanking, signed in 1842, ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain, opened the five treaty ports of Shanghai, Guangzhou, Ningbo, Fuzhou, and Xiamen, and required China to pay 21 million silver dollars.

From 1856 to 1860 Britain and France waged the Second Opium War against China, resulting in the Treaties of Tianjin (1858) and Peking (1860); the second phase of fighting included the sack of the Old Summer Palace and the occupation of the Forbidden City palace complex in Beijing.

China ceded sovereignty over Hong Kong to the British Empire, whose control over the territory lasted until 1997. To remember the Opium Wars, recall 1840, the destruction of opium at Humen, the Treaty of Nanking, and the cession of Hong Kong.
Another achievement of the Liangzhu culture was the advent of silk, a precious legacy it left to later ages. The silk ribbons and silk fabric from Qianshanyang are the most direct evidence.

Archaeologists found silk ribbons and silk cloth stored in bamboo baskets at Qianshanyang — major physical evidence of early silkworm raising and silk weaving in China. Together with rice farming and animal husbandry, they show the fairly diversified economy of the time.

The grave goods of cemeteries such as Yaoshan also hint at textile production: the northern row of Yaoshan tombs contained jade huang pendants and spinning wheels, in contrast with the jade cong and yue of the southern row — a difference generally read as one of gender.

When you look at the silk textiles and related burial goods in the collection, imagine the strand of silk carried from a bamboo basket to the present day: five thousand years ago, the watery lands of Jiangnan had already begun to raise silkworms and weave silk.
