blocks.text: The 'Four Great Inventions' is a concept in the history of Chinese science and technology referring to four inventions of ancient China: papermaking, the compass, gunpowder, and printing. The American scholar Thomas Francis Carter first set out the idea explicitly in the preface of his 1925 book The Invention of Printing in China and Its Spread Westward.

Papermaking is traditionally attributed to Cai Lun, a court eunuch of the Eastern Han, but archeological evidence shows that paper existed earlier; Cai Lun was an important improver and developer of the craft. The forerunner of the compass was the ancient Chinese south-pointing ladle (sinan); in his Dream Pool Essays of 1088, the Northern Song polymath Shen Kuo was the first to describe magnetic declination accurately.

The earliest known written record of a gunpowder formula appears in the Essentials of the Military Classics of 1044, from the Song dynasty. The earliest woodblock-printed work yet found is the Dharani Sutra published between 650 and 670; the Diamond Sutra, printed in 868 during the Tang, is the earliest known printed book of ordinary size; and movable type is said to have been invented by Bi Sheng of the Northern Song, who used baked clay pieces.

China used practical firearms some five centuries before Europe; the compass reached the Arab world around the turn of the 13th century and was passed on from there to Europe. To remember the Four Great Inventions, recall papermaking, the compass, gunpowder, and printing.

The jade used for Liangzhu objects came mainly from the tremolite deposits of Xiaomeiling in the Tianmu range, Liyang, Jiangsu. Jade-working workshops have been found at the Tangshanbei site within the Liangzhu cluster and at Dingshadi in Jurong, Jiangsu.

blocks.caption: Liangzhu Jade Craftsmanship and Sources of Jade

blocks.text: The Tangshan site in Yuhang had a jade workshop that yielded more than 400 stone tools for jade working, including whetstones, grinding and polishing stones, and carving tools, along with over 100 pieces of jade waste, most bearing traces of workmanship. Three workshop structures built of stone blocks have also been identified.

Making Liangzhu jade was extraordinarily difficult, above all the intricate beast-mask motifs, in which three incised lines pass within a single millimetre. Objects like these must have been produced by full-time, even hereditary craftsmen released from agriculture — evidence that Liangzhu society had already developed a specialized class of artisans.

As you look at the jades, trace them from the mines of Liyang through the many stages of the workshop. A single piece of tremolite is among the most powerful evidence of specialization in Liangzhu's craft industry.

c41fc4b3-78f5-534f-8d98-5f4e27f31247.name: Liangzhu Jade Craftsmanship and Sources of Jade

blocks.text: Wang Anshi (1021–1086), courtesy name Jiefu and sobriquet Banshan, was a native of Linchuan county in Fuzhou. A Northern Song statesman, writer, thinker, and reformer, he was created Duke of Jing and posthumously honored as Wen; posterity counts him among the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song. In the third month of the second year of Qingli (1042), at the age of twenty-two, he passed the jinshi examination.

While magistrate of Yin county, Wang Anshi lent grain from the official granaries to the people, repaid with interest after the autumn harvest; the Green Sprouts policy he later championed grew directly out of this practice. In the second year of Xining (1069), Emperor Shenzong appointed him vice grand councilor, and in the twelfth month of the third year of Xining (1070) he rose to grand councilor. The reforms he led are known in history as the Xining Reforms or Wang Anshi's Reforms.

Across the realm Wang Anshi implemented new laws including the Green Sprouts policy, the Farmland and Water Conservancy law, and the Replacement Service law, and reformed the examination system, the bureaucracy, and the military, also introducing the mutual-responsibility baojia system. He was dismissed from office twice, in 1074 and 1076.

After Emperor Shenzong's death, Sima Guang became grand councilor and led the Yuanyou reversal, repealing nearly all of the reform laws. Wang Anshi died at Jiangning Prefecture in 1086 (the first year of Yuanyou), aged sixty-four. To remember him, recall the Green Sprouts policy, the Xining Reforms, his two dismissals from office, and his place among the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song.

The guqin (seven-stringed zither) is one of the oldest instruments in Chinese history and an object through which the Chinese have given voice to sound and feeling. On 7 November 2003, the art of the guqin was inscribed by UNESCO on the second Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity; on 20 May 2006, the State Council added the guqin to the first national list of intangible cultural heritage.

blocks.caption: The Guqin and the Chinese World of Sound

blocks.text: Guqin making advanced enormously in the Tang dynasty. The 'Jiuxiao Huanpei' and 'Dasheng Yiyin' zithers made for the Tang imperial family by the Lei family of Sichuan are both famous surviving instruments, and Tang zithers have been prized in every age as rare treasures. Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated examples are those made in the Tang, and nearly twenty Tang instruments survive today. As for form, the old saying holds that 'the Tang is round'.

In the Song and Yuan periods distinct schools of guqin began to emerge. The first school, the Zhe school, appeared in the late Southern Song, founded by Guo Mian. Today more than 3,360 guqin pieces, over 130 tablature collections and some 300 guqin songs survive.

Before the guqin cases at the Zhejiang Museum, grow quiet first: study the crackle patterns and inscriptions on the instruments, then consider how an object spanning 'from Tang to Song, from the Lei family to the Zhe school' keeps an aural tradition alive on a wooden body lacquered over.

c5978321-c18b-582e-bcac-e1990d4561ac.name: The Guqin and the Chinese World of Sound

blocks.text: The Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue is a bronze sword cast during the reign of King Zhejiyushi of the Spring and Autumn period. It is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. Although Zhejiyushi reigned for only six years, he had bronze swords cast in great numbers.

blocks.caption: The Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue

blocks.text: King Zhejiyushi of Yue is the Shiyu recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian as the son of King Goujian. His name appears as 'Yuyi' in the Yue Jue Shu and as 'Luying' in the Bamboo Annals. According to the Bamboo Annals, Luying reigned for six years, from 464 to 459 BC in the Western calendar.

Swords of this kind reflect many facets of the bronze smelting and casting technology of the Wu-Yue region. Inscribed Yue king swords are relatively rare finds and are usually works of superb craftsmanship. Known examples bear the names of the kings Goujian, Zhejiyushi, Bushou, Zhougou, Buguang and Jibeigu.

When you view this sword, first read the inscription on the blade or the guard, then reflect on its owner's story - a son of Goujian who reigned six years yet cast swords in profusion for posterity. A single weapon thus links the Records of the Grand Historian with an object before your eyes.

c93861c2-1ccb-5cc1-a394-e3e67da38c5d.name: The Sword of King Zhejiyushi of Yue

blocks.text: The Kaiyuan flourishing age, also called the Kaiyuan golden rule, was the golden age of the Tang under Emperor Xuanzong. For the first thirty years of his governance Xuanzong used the era name Kaiyuan, governing with vigor and appointing worthy and able men, and raised the Tang to the summit of its power.

After ascending the throne, Xuanzong first appointed Yao Chong and Song Jing as chancellors, then Zhang Jiazhen, Zhang Yue, Li Yuanhong, Du Xian, Han Xiu, and Zhang Jiuling in turn. By the first year of Tianbao (742), the Tang empire's population had reached about 48.91 million.

Adopting the proposal of Zhang Yue, Emperor Xuanzong implemented a volunteer-based standing army to replace the declining fubing garrison system. In the first year of Tianbao (742) he established ten frontier military commands under military governors (jiedushi), intended as a deterrent against foreign peoples and a measure of border defense — but they also planted the seeds of the An Lushan Rebellion that later erupted.

The Kaiyuan flourishing age was the summit of the Tang, lying close to the turning point of decline after prosperity. To remember it, recall the chancellors Yao Chong and Song Jing, the population of about 48.91 million, and the military governors who sowed the seeds of the An Lushan Rebellion.

The Fanshan aristocratic cemetery lies near the ancient Liangzhu city. It is a deliberately built and finished platform cemetery, about 100 metres east–west and 30 metres north–south. Every tomb has its burial pit, and the grave goods, chiefly jade, number about a thousand pieces in total.

Tomb 20 at Fanshan contained as many as 547 jade objects and is thought to be the burial of the supreme leader. Tomb 12 yielded a jade cong weighing 3,500 grams and carved with delicate beast-mask motifs, regarded as the 'King of Cong'; it also yielded an exceptionally well-made jade yue, the 'King of Yue', mounted on a 70–80 cm wooden haft fitted with jade fittings at both ends — a symbol of military and royal power.

The jade from the great tombs of Fanshan and Yaoshan is genuine nephrite, in contrast with the jade used in lesser cemeteries. Yan Wenming believed that the aristocratic cemeteries of Fanshan and Yaoshan may well have been the royal tombs of the Liangzhu 'kingdom'. In February 1989, the Fanshan and Yaoshan sites were both named among China's Top Ten Archaeological Discoveries of the Seventh Five-Year Plan period.

In the Fanshan protected area of the site park, walk back and forth along the hundred-odd-metre terrace. Feel how densely the burial jades are concentrated here — beneath a single terrace lie leader after leader with their world of jade ritual.

The Southern Song Guan Kiln Campus of the Hangzhou West Lake Museum (formerly the Southern Song Guan Kiln Museum) is located in Hangzhou, Zhejiang. Built on the site of the Southern Song imperial kiln at Jiaotanxia, it is the first museum in China devoted to ceramics and built around an ancient kiln site, and the most direct place to learn about the Southern Song Guan kiln.

The Southern Song Guan Kiln Museum covers about 43,000 square metres with 10,000 square metres of exhibition space. It opened to the public in 1992, underwent comprehensive renovation in 2002, a second-phase expansion in 2007, and completed a third-phase expansion in 2010. In April 2020 it was merged with the Hangzhou West Lake Museum and the Hangzhou Museum of Famous People into the Hangzhou West Lake Museum headquarters.

Founded on the Jiaotanxia kiln site in Hangzhou, the Southern Song Guan kiln, together with the Yue and Longquan kilns, forms a key link in the genealogy of Zhejiang celadon. Southern Song Guan celadon is also an important part of the ceramic collection of the Zhejiang Museum.

If, after visiting the Zhejiang Museum, you still want to go deeper into the history of ceramics, make a special trip to the Southern Song Guan Kiln Campus at the Jiaotanxia site, where kiln site and galleries stand together - there you can go from firing temperatures and glazes all the way to the remains of the kilns themselves.

Huang Binhong (27 January 1865 - 25 March 1955), personal name Zhi, courtesy names Pucun and Puren, and known by the sobriquets Yuxiang, Honglu and Hongsou, adopted the name Binhong in middle age and is known by it. Born in Jinhua, Zhejiang, with ancestral roots in Tandu village, western She County, Anhui, he was a modern Chinese landscape painter.

blocks.caption: Huang Binhong and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: On 22 March 1955, Huang Binhong's family donated his collections: 1,848 titles of books, 2,416 letters, 810 manuscripts, 10 genealogies, 65 records of painting appraisal at the Palace Museum and 6 volumes of decipherings of ancient seals. According to another account, after Huang's death his family, honouring his last wish, donated all the more than five thousand of his works and over ten thousand artefacts, manuscripts and other belongings to the Zhejiang Museum.

In March 1958, the Zhejiang Museum established the Huang Binhong Memorial Room at No. 31 Qixia Ridge, Hangzhou. In the summer of 1948, the 85-year-old Huang, invited by the National Hangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, came south from Beiping and spent the last seven years of his life here. The memorial room formally opened to visitors in 1988.

When you see Huang Binhong's many works and manuscripts in the museum's painting and calligraphy galleries, reflect: this painter, who in his later years pursued a style of 'depth, richness, splendour and vitality', left his life's work to Zhejiang and became one of the great pillars of the museum's collection.

d402f589-b0e2-59f7-96ee-d53df0019cb1.name: Huang Binhong and the Zhejiang Museum

d4218a8d-f8be-5b37-bf25-a4e32d7c28cf.name: Qianwang Temple and the Wuyue Kingdom

blocks.text: Shi Xingeng (1912–1939) was born in Liangzhu town, Hang County, Zhejiang (today's Yuhang District). A geologist–mineralogist and archaeologist, he was the first to carry out scientific excavation at the Liangzhu site, and is honoured as an outstanding pioneer of exploration into the Liangzhu culture.

blocks.caption: Shi Xingeng and the Discovery of Liangzhu

blocks.text: On 31 May 1936, Shi Xingeng took part in a test excavation of the Gudang site at the request of the West Lake Museum. Noticing that some of the stone tools collected 'were a common sight in my hometown', the next day he returned to the Liangzhu area in search of Neolithic sites. On 3 November 1936, at the bottom of a pond at Qipanfen near Liangzhu town, he found two pieces of shiny black pottery.

Between December 1936 and March 1937, Shi Xingeng carried out three test excavations around Liangzhu, identifying twelve sites including Maoanli and Qipanfen. In April 1937 he completed the book Liangzhu: A Preliminary Report on the Black Pottery Culture Sites of the Second District of Hang County, published in Shanghai by the China Science Corporation in August 1938. On 29 May 1939, Shi Xingeng died of scarlet fever complicated by peritonitis, aged just 28.

In the 'Discovery and the Pursuit of Truth' section of the Liangzhu Museum, remember that this young archaeologist, who died of illness at 28, is the starting point of the whole story. The two pieces of black pottery he found would unveil an entire prehistoric civilization of Jiangnan.

d48d7adb-49d2-5879-9dd2-381f6bc9f06a.name: Shi Xingeng and the Discovery of Liangzhu

blocks.text: The Five Dynasties Wuyue gilded silver Asoka Pagoda is one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum. A small pagoda-shaped artefact of the jewel casket stupa type, it came from the excavation of the Leifeng Pagoda site.

blocks.caption: The Five Dynasties Gilded Silver Asoka Pagoda

blocks.text: The underground palace of Leifeng Pagoda, opened on 11 March 2001, was a brick-built vertical shaft. At its centre stood an iron reliquary casket, surrounded by offerings symbolizing the 'Seven Treasures' and other Buddhist artefacts. Altogether 51 groups of objects were unearthed from the underground palace, the most important being a gilded pure-silver Asoka Pagoda. Inside its body was a golden container wrapped with thin gold leaf into the shape of a coffin, presumably enshrining a relic of the Buddha's spiral hair. Together with the pure-silver Asoka Pagoda, it ranks among the most important objects from the site.

Both Asoka pagodas are square in form, composed of a base, a body, four banana-leaf-like 'mountain flowers' and a spire, with scenes from the Buddha's jataka (past-life) stories engraved on all four sides of the body. Most of the many artefacts unearthed at Leifeng Pagoda in 2000-2001 are now collected and displayed at the Zhejiang Museum.

As you look at this gilded little pagoda, first take in the banana-leaf corners and the engraved scenes on its body, then recall that it rested at the very centre of the Leifeng Pagoda underground palace for a thousand years - the most direct physical evidence of the Wuyue Buddhist kingdom and of the pagoda history of Hangzhou.

d8cac2ce-ce89-5d8d-b041-07fd586c9fc7.name: The Five Dynasties Gilded Silver Asoka Pagoda

blocks.text: The outer water-management system of Liangzhu was part of its monumental engineering, made up of high dams in the valley mouths, low dams on the plain and a long embankment along the foothills. Together they represent some of the earliest waterworks in China.

The high dams in the valley mouths lie at the southern foot of the Dazhe mountains, northwest of the city, covering about 136.41 hectares. There are six dams in two groups, east and west, each 50–200 metres long, with crests at 25–40 metres above sea level. The low dams on the plain lie among hills about 3.5 kilometres south of the high dams, each 35–360 metres long, with crests at about 10 metres above sea level. The long embankment along the foothills, also known as the Tangshan site, runs along the north of the ancient city for about 5 kilometres and is 20–50 metres wide. In 2015, the survey and excavation of this outer water-management project was named one of China's Top Ten Archaeological Discoveries.

Cho-yun Hsu believed that Liangzhu's complex social system emerged in response to the need for collective, cooperative flood control, not from military conquest. Together with the Mojiaoshan terrace and the city walls, this water system shows that Liangzhu could mobilize large numbers of workers to organize water management.

When you visit the site park, don't only walk inside the city. Notice the line of dams and embankments stretching north of it; together with the walls and terraces, they complete the picture of how the Liangzhu people managed water and settled.

Zheng He (1371–1433), originally surnamed Ma with the childhood name Sanbao, was a native of Kunyang in Yunnan. The Yongle emperor bestowed on him the surname Zheng, whence his name. A military officer, navigator, diplomat, and eunuch of the Ming, he led seven great voyages at the Yongle emperor's command over twenty-eight years, visiting more than thirty countries and regions along the western Pacific and Indian Ocean — the voyages known in history as Zheng He's journeys to the Western Ocean, covering more than 70,000 nautical miles in all.

On the fifteenth day of the sixth month in the third year of Yongle (July 11, 1405), the Yongle emperor ordered Zheng He to lead a fleet of more than 240 ocean-going ships with 27,400 crewmen on a voyage to distant seas. On his fourth voyage he rounded the Arabian Peninsula and for the first time sailed as far as Malindi in present-day Kenya, East Africa.

Zheng He reached more than thirty states, including Java, Sumatra, Sulu, Malacca, Chenla, Siam, Hormuz, and Mogadishu, venturing as far as the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea. On his seventh voyage he died in 1433 (eighth year of Xuande) at Calicut on the west coast of India.

Since 2005, July 11 of each year has been observed in China as National Maritime Day, chosen to mark the date of Zheng He's first voyage, July 11, 1405. To remember Zheng He, recall his seven voyages, visits to more than thirty countries, and the journeys that reached as far as the east coast of Africa.

e03453b8-6b6a-53ef-9a91-b26aa83f2120.name: The Layout of West Lake: One Hill, Two Pagodas, Three Isles

e2d63219-cc30-5605-8cb5-e3795f3bf2aa.name: Buddhist Temple Culture of West Lake

blocks.text: The Liangzhu culture already possessed writing in the making, or proto-writing. Not a mature script, it nevertheless shows recognizable symbols, and is one of the keys to understanding Liangzhu's path toward 'civilization'.

Li Xueqin once identified fourteen signs, including those for 'bird', 'sun', 'seal', 'swallow' and 'mountain'; some resemble the pottery symbols of the Dawenkou culture. In 2013, the archaeologist Xu Xinmin discovered still more written symbols while cataloguing finds from the Zhuangqiaofen site in Pinghu, Zhejiang.

These incised symbols often appear on jade, pottery and other objects, showing that beyond shaping form, the Liangzhu people had begun to express things with signs — one of the early forms of Chinese writing.

As you search the exhibits for those carved birds and pointed signs, reflect: five thousand years ago, people were already recording language in lines — a step taken earlier here than in many other regions.

This memorial room preserves the late-life studio of Huang Binhong, the modern landscape master who lived beside West Lake. His family donated over five thousand works to the Zhejiang Museum, forming a pillar of its painting collection.

In the Zhejiang across Ten Thousand Years exhibition at the Zhejiang Provincial Museum (Zhijiang Hall), several treasures of the Liangzhu culture are placed in prominent positions — the most important opening chapter of Zhejiang's memory of 'jade ritual'.

blocks.caption: Liangzhu at the Zhejiang Provincial Museum

blocks.text: The museum's collection includes Hemudu pottery, jades and silks, as well as Liangzhu jades. Among its ten greatest treasures is a 'Liangzhu culture jade cong', and the list of relics prohibited from travelling abroad includes the King Jade Cong excavated from Liangzhu, held by the Zhejiang Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology.

If you have already visited the Liangzhu Museum, you will recognize in Zhejiang this same system of jades from the tombs; if not, the ancient state of Liangzhu is introduced here in the friendliest of ways.

When you see Liangzhu at Zhejiang, link it to the route of Zhejiang across Ten Thousand Years — from the King Jade Cong to the Liangzhu cong, the earliest thread of Zhejiang civilization unfolds before you.

e45da344-5dfc-5602-b582-33f67c8a312c.name: Liangzhu at the Zhejiang Provincial Museum

blocks.text: Zhang Cheng's carved red-lacquer plate of children at play is a work by the master Yuan lacquer carver Zhang Cheng. It ranks as a national-treasure-grade artefact, one of only four known pieces bearing the mark 'made by Zhang Cheng', and the crowning piece of the Zhejiang Museum's lacquer collection.

blocks.caption: Zhang Cheng's Carved Red-Lacquer Plate of Children at Play

blocks.text: The carved red-lacquer plate of children at play by Zhang Cheng, master carver of the Yuan, is a national-treasure-grade work and one of only four known pieces 'made by Zhang Cheng'. In 2012, the noted Zhejiang-born Hong Kong industrialist Mr. Cao Qiyong and his wife donated 160 pieces (groups) of lacquerware they had treasured for years to the Zhejiang Museum - and this plate was among them.

Appraisal found that the donated lacquerware includes 21 first-grade, 118 second-grade and 15 third-grade artefacts. Among the gifts, the plain one-colour lacquer of the Song and Yuan, the carved ribbed (tixi) lacquer of the early Ming, the incised-gold inlaid lacquer of the Jiajing and Wanli reigns, and the mid-Qing wares represented by Qianlong's reign are all extremely precious examples of the art.

As you look at this plate, first take in the children-at-play design carved after layer upon layer of lacquer was applied, then consider how this piece of carved lacquer passed from a Yuan craftsman's hands to the present day and into the Zhejiang Museum through the Cao donation - craftsman, collector and museum, all joined by a single lacquer object.

e50f9576-9d0d-506d-a71d-e893854c5e5f.name: Zhang Cheng's Carved Red-Lacquer Plate of Children at Play

e58c5e31-a4b0-5cac-bc18-58a88dda0fe6.name: Three Pools on the One-Yuan Banknote

blocks.text: The cong is a cylindrical jade object used for sacrifice in ancient China, shaped rather like a brush pot, square outside and round inside. The earliest jade cong is found in the third phase of the Xuejiagang culture at Qianshan, Anhui, dating to about 5100 years ago.

blocks.caption: The Cong: A Ritual Object Linking Heaven and Earth

blocks.text: Among jade objects, the cong was used for worshipping the earth. The ancients held that 'the heavens are round and the earth square', so round bi discs honoured heaven and square cong honoured earth. The Rites of Zhou records: 'Six jade objects were made to ritualize heaven, earth and the four directions: a blue-green bi to honour heaven, a yellow cong to honour the earth.'

Liangzhu cong are hollow cylinders within, and the hollow centre is thought to be a passage linking the gods of heaven and earth. Hayashi Minao believed the beast mask on the cong represented a sun god or fire god, while Li Xueqin held it to be a dragon. Even the very function of the cong was not settled by the Qing dynasty: the Qianlong Emperor once used excavated cong as counterweights for moving heavy objects.

When you look at a cong in the museum, remember just four words: 'square outside, round within'. The square is the earth, the circle is heaven — in a single cong, the ancient imagination of cosmic order lies in your hands.

e5ac2ef8-9095-57a6-808c-43df7159b392.name: The Cong: A Ritual Object Linking Heaven and Earth

blocks.text: Wuyue (16 June 907 - 9 June 978) was one of the Ten Kingdoms of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period. Founded by Qian Liu in 907 with its capital at Hangzhou (the 'Western Capital'), it was the only state never conquered by force during the Northern Song's founding wars.

blocks.caption: The Wuyue Kingdom and Its Policy of Protecting the Realm

blocks.text: At the height of its power Wuyue ruled thirteen prefectures, roughly corresponding to the whole of today's Zhejiang province, southeastern Jiangsu and northeastern Fujian. From 902, when Emperor Zhaozong of Tang enfeoffed Qian Liu as King of Yue, to 978, when Qian Chu surrendered to the Northern Song, Wuyue passed through five kings over 72 years. On 9 June 978, Qian Hongchu offered his territory to the Song, bringing the Wuyue regime to an end.

Pressed by the landward military threats of the neighbouring Wu kingdom and the Southern Tang, Wuyue vigorously developed maritime trade. The Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties records that boats crowded the capital Hangzhou 'so densely that neither bow nor stern could be seen'; the Northern Song writer Su Shi called its wealth in ivory, rhinoceros horn, pearls and jade 'the finest under heaven'. Under a policy of protecting the realm and reassuring the people, the economy prospered, and the profits of fishing, salt, sericulture and mulberry farming surpassed all of Jiangnan.

In the Wuyue and Song gallery of 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang', picture Leifeng Pagoda, Baochu Pagoda and the surrounding West Lake relics as the skyline of the Wuyue kingdom - a realm that prospered through seafaring and stability, and the very image of Zhejiang in the Five Dynasties.

e84ba7e7-7bc1-5891-ab65-edadd0f34cc9.name: The Wuyue Kingdom and Its Policy of Protecting the Realm

ec78e61f-e1cf-551a-a597-57e9ecff9f22.name: The Qianlong Emperor and West Lake

blocks.text: The Jin was divided into the Western Jin and the Eastern Jin, together called the Two Jins. The Western Jin (265–316), founded by Emperor Wu (Sima Yan), had its capital at Luoyang; the Eastern Jin (317–420), founded by Emperor Yuan (Sima Rui), had its capital at Jiankang (present-day Nanjing, Jiangsu). Together the Two Jins lasted 154 years.

In 280 the Western Jin conquered Sun Wu and unified the realm, but peace and stability lasted barely a decade. After Emperor Hui ascended the throne, the princely lords rebelled in what is known as the War of the Eight Princes; in 311 Liu Cong, Wang Mi, and Shi Le sacked Luoyang in the disaster known as the Yongjia catastrophe, and in 316 the Western Jin fell, plunging the north into the period of the Sixteen Kingdoms of the Five Barbarian peoples.

In 317 Sima Rui proclaimed himself emperor at Jiankang, beginning the Eastern Jin; the aristocratic families and common people of the Central Plains migrated south in waves, an event recorded as the 'southern migration of robes and caps'. In 383, at the Battle of the Fei River, the Eastern Jin's 80,000-strong Beifu army routed the vast forces of Fu Jian of the Former Qin.

In 420 Liu Yu deposed Emperor Gong of Jin and established himself as ruler of the Liu Song, ending the Eastern Jin and opening the Northern and Southern Dynasties period. To remember the Two Jins, recall the brief Western Jin unification, the War of the Eight Princes, the southern migration of the elite, and the Battle of the Fei River.

f097d527-52d8-568b-890c-1325f4b99a40.name: Southern Song Lin'an and the Ten Scenes

blocks.text: The Zhijiang Campus is the new main venue of the Zhejiang Museum. Located in the Zhijiang Cultural Center of Hangzhou, it opened to the public on 29 August 2023, covering about 54,400 square metres with a floor area of 100,000 square metres.

blocks.caption: The Zhijiang Campus and 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang'

blocks.text: Its core is the permanent exhibition 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture', spread over the first and second floors and divided into three galleries: 'From Prehistory to the Sui and Tang Dynasties', 'Wuyue and the Two Song Dynasties', and 'From the Yuan, Ming and Qing Dynasties to the Modern Era'. It traces Zhejiang's history from the Paleolithic to 1921 and opened in August 2023. All five groups of artefacts on the national list prohibited from exhibition abroad are on display in this exhibition.

The third floor also houses the permanent exhibition 'Eastward Lies the Ocean - Zhejiang's Maritime Culture', covering about 1,000 square metres. The galleries below the third floor are arranged in chronological order, offering a complementary thread alongside 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang'.

For most visitors, the Zhijiang Campus is the smoothest entry point to the whole of Zhejiang's history: follow the three galleries from prehistory to the modern era, then turn back to examine the museum's treasures and the artefacts barred from overseas exhibition - and the thread of ten thousand years becomes clear.

f1967937-d54e-5f3a-8492-b74f2d81f6a9.name: The Zhijiang Campus and 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang'

blocks.text: The Song dynasty (960–1279), divided into the Northern Song and the Southern Song and together called the Two Songs, lasted 319 years — the longest-ruling Chinese dynasty since the establishment of the imperial institution. In 960 Zhao Kuangyin became emperor through the Chenqiao mutiny, taking the name Song Taizu, with the dynastic title Song and the capital at Kaifeng.

At the founding of the dynasty, Taizu reclaimed military power for the central court 'over a cup of wine' and pursued a national policy of elevating civilian culture while curbing the military. In 1004 the Song and Liao made peace at the walls of Chanzhou: the Song paid the Liao an annual tribute of 200,000 bolts of silk and 100,000 taels of silver, and the two states became 'brother nations' — an agreement known as the Treaty of Chanyuan.

In 1127 the Jin conquered the Northern Song in the Jingkang Incident; Prince Kang, Zhao Gou, took the throne at Yingtian Prefecture, beginning the Southern Song. According to the scholar Angus Maddison, the Song accounted for 22.7% of world economic output at the time; all Four Great Inventions were refined, and six of the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song came from the Song.

In 1276 Lin'an fell, and in 1279 the Song fleet was annihilated at the Battle of Yamen, ending the dynasty. To remember the Song, recall the policy of favoring civil over martial affairs, the Treaty of Chanyuan, the Jingkang Incident, and the age's economic and technological brilliance.

The Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods are the historical subdivisions of the Eastern Zhou: the Spring and Autumn period generally refers to 770–476 BC; the start of the Warring States period is dated variously, with common markers being 475 BC or 403 BC, when the Zhou king formally recognized Han, Zhao, and Wei as feudal lords; the period ends with Qin's unification of the six states in 221 BC.

The Spring and Autumn period takes its name from the Annals, the chronicle edited by Confucius. It was an age of drastic transformation in Chinese social institutions, marked by the widespread use of iron and a gradual entry into the Iron Age. Daoist, Confucian, and Mohist schools of thought had already appeared by the late Spring and Autumn period, and by the mid-Warring States the Hundred Schools of Thought contended freely.

In 453 BC Han, Zhao, and Wei jointly destroyed the Zhi clan, and in 403 BC King Weilie of Zhou formally invested the three houses as feudal lords — the event known as the Partition of Jin. In 386 BC Tian He was recognized by the Zhou court as Marquis of Qi, and the Tian clan replaced the Jiang-surnamed house of Qi. Han, Zhao, Wei, Qi, Qin, Chu, and Yan are known together as the Seven Powers of the Warring States. In 356 BC Duke Xiao of Qin employed Shang Yang to carry out reforms, and in 260 BC the Battle of Changping between Qin and Zhao ended in a crushing defeat for Zhao.

The Spring and Autumn and Warring States period closed with Qin's unification of the six states. It was an era of contending powers and a hundred schools of thought, a time of radical transformation in China's political institutions and social thought; remember the phrases 'Five Hegemons of the Spring and Autumn', 'Seven Powers of the Warring States', and 'Shang Yang's reforms' to sketch its outline.

The Hemudu culture was a Neolithic culture distributed across the plains on the southern shore of Hangzhou Bay in Zhejiang, China, extending to the Zhoushan Islands, dating from roughly 6,000 to 7,000 years ago. It takes its name from the Hemudu site in Yuyao, where it was first excavated.

The site has yielded extensive remains of stilt houses (ganlan buildings) and cultivated rice, along with plant remains such as gourds, acorns, water chestnuts and jujubes, and domestic animals including pigs, dogs and water buffalo. Stone tools are relatively few; wood and bone implements predominate. Among the finds are China's earliest wooden ornament, a carved wooden fish, and the earliest lacquerware yet discovered in China.

The Hemudu culture was first identified in 1973, and the Hemudu site was excavated in two campaigns in 1973-1974 and 1977-1978. In the 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang' exhibition at the Zhijiang Campus, Hemudu pottery, bone ploughs and lacquered woodwork are often among the first artefacts visitors encounter.

As you face the Hemudu exhibits, ponder this: stilt houses, cultivated rice and domesticated animals all appear together, showing that the people here already knew how to run their own lives in the watery landscape of Hangzhou Bay six or seven thousand years ago.

The Liangzhu Ancient City Archaeological Site Park is an archaeological park centred on the ancient Liangzhu city. On this World Heritage land, you can see directly the city, the walls, the water system and the royal tombs of five thousand years ago.

blocks.caption: Liangzhu Ancient City Archaeological Site Park

blocks.text: The park is built around the ancient Liangzhu city site, covering the palatial zone on the Mojiaoshan terrace, the inner and outer cities, the outer water-management system and the Fanshan aristocratic cemetery. On 9 October 2010, the State Administration of Cultural Heritage named the Liangzhu site among the first batch of national archaeological site parks. This is the place where more than five thousand years of Chinese civilization is demonstrated most directly.

Before you tour, mark the Mojiaoshan terrace (about 30 hectares) and the Fanshan royal tombs on your map. As you walk, keep checking the waterways and the palatial zone against your position, and you will avoid seeing only scattered terraces.

Walking across this open land, try to read the rising heights of the Mojiaoshan terrace, the outer city and the inner city as a gradient visible to the naked eye — perhaps the most direct way to understand Liangzhu as an 'early city'.

fdb68b9b-f4ed-5637-9e3a-4c09f9f6d4ca.name: Liangzhu Ancient City Archaeological Site Park

blocks.text: Standing on the wall at Badaling, first look east and west along the battlements: this section belongs to the Ming wall system. The wall that survives today is chiefly the Ming Great Wall, begun in the 14th century and running from Jiayuguan in the west to the Hushan wall in the east.

Through twenty large-scale construction campaigns the Ming built a wall stretching 8,851.8 kilometers from Jiayuguan in Gansu to Hushan in Liaoning, running largely along the line of the Nine Border Commands. The wall system consists chiefly of four parts: passes, walls and towers, and beacon towers.

In 1987 the Great Wall was inscribed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site. Counting its eastern and western sections and its successive passes together, the entire wall stretches over ten thousand li — roughly 4,500 to 6,000 kilometers.

From the wall at Badaling, set the phrase 'Wall of Ten Thousand Li' back in time: it began to be built during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, the First Emperor's joining of the old walls earned it the name 'Ten Thousand Li Wall', and the Ming wall is the most complete part surviving today.

In this tour of the Zhijiang Campus, bring your gaze back to a single painting: the 'Remaining Mountain Scroll' of the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains. When you view it, first look at the short opening section left by the fire, then at the texts and digital reconstructions beside it, and imagine what the originally complete long scroll of the Fuchun River must have looked like.

The Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains is the work of Huang Gongwang, a painter active at the end of the Song and beginning of the Yuan, painted between 1347 and 1350 against the backdrop of the Fuchun River in Zhejiang. It is his masterpiece, praised by later generations as the 'Lanting of painting' and the 'supreme divine work of landscape painting', and one of China's ten greatest surviving paintings. The small opening section, repaired, is known as the 'Remaining Mountain Scroll', 51.4 cm wide and 31.8 cm high, about one-fourteenth of the original; the longer section is the 'Scroll for Master Wuyong', 636.9 cm wide and 33 cm high, about twelve-fourteenths of the original.

The Remaining Mountain Scroll and the Scroll for Master Wuyong were shown at the Taipei palace museum on 2 June 2011, but the two reunited originals were not joined together; instead they were displayed side by side in a single case sixteen metres long. The Zhejiang Museum treasures precisely the Remaining Mountain Scroll, and it, too, was chosen among the museum's top ten treasures.

0abc9dd1-6c4c-5aa8-905c-1af7c3a2aab2.name: Between Mountain and Water: The Digital Exhibition of the Dwelling in the Fuchun Mountains

blocks.text: The Fanshan site in the park is a high-terrace cemetery of royal rank within Liangzhu's aristocratic burial grounds — about 100 metres east–west and 30 metres north–south, an artificially built and finished terrace.

Fanshan's grave goods, chiefly jade, number about a thousand pieces in total. Tomb 20 contained as many as 547 jade objects and is thought to be the burial of the supreme leader; Tomb 12 yielded the King Jade Cong and the King Jade Yue. Yan Wenming believed this may indeed have been the site of the Liangzhu royal tombs.

As you visit, compare it with the Mojiaoshan terrace in the same park: one terrace held the palace of the capital, the other the royal tombs of the aristocracy. Only together do the two complete the three-dimensional picture of the 'Liangzhu kingdom'.
Standing on the Fanshan terrace, think of those '547 pieces of jade' — beneath a single terrace lies a world of power built of jade.

The 'Discovery and the Pursuit of Truth' section opens the museum's three-part display — 'Discovery, the Ancient State, Civilization' — and from here you can follow, step by step, how Liangzhu came to be 'seen'.

The Liangzhu site was discovered in 1936, when Shi Xingeng of the West Lake Museum found shiny black pottery at Qipanfen near Liangzhu, Yuhang, and carried out three test excavations; in 1938 he published Liangzhu. In 1959 the archaeologist Xia Nai gave the culture its name, 'Liangzhu culture'. The successive excavations at Fanshan, Yaoshan and Mojiaoshan that followed mark the milestones of our knowledge of Liangzhu.

This story is full of milestones: Huiguanshan in 1991, Mojiaoshan in 1993, the discovery of the ancient city in 2007, and the survey of the outer water system in 2015, among others — many of them named among China's Top Ten Archaeological Discoveries. The few steps you take through this gallery correspond to decades of fieldwork.

As you read this section, set the dates 1936–1959–2019 as a timeline in your mind; from a single piece of black pottery to a World Heritage site, the excavation story of this Jiangnan land gains its depth.

1e71581c-11c2-5eb7-8643-773d0c08a4f5.name: Discovery and the Pursuit of Truth: The Story of the Excavations

blocks.text: Before the guqin cases, there is no need to rush to the labels. Grow quiet first: study the crackle patterns, inscriptions and names on the instruments, then listen for the faint audio cues by the cases, and you will feel how the guqin, as a 'tradition of listening', has been preserved on a wooden body lacquered over.

The art of the guqin was inscribed by UNESCO on the second Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity on 7 November 2003. On 20 May 2006, the State Council added the guqin to the first national intangible cultural heritage list, classified under 'folk music', number II-34.

Among surviving guqin, the earliest reliably dated are those of the Tang dynasty; nearly twenty Tang zithers survive today and have been treasured in every age. In the Song and Yuan periods distinct schools of guqin began to emerge; the first, the Zhe school, appeared in the late Southern Song, founded by Guo Mian. The Tang seven-stringed zither 'Cai Feng Ming Qi', one of the top ten treasures of the Zhejiang Museum, belongs to this group of surviving Tang instruments.

3fc8e5c1-c715-5ba8-b0df-2011a9adc717.name: Sound of Antiquity: The Guqin Gallery

blocks.text: At the gate of Sha Menghai's former residence, first look at the five-character plaque on the stone wall inside the courtyard, then take in the brick-and-timber structure of this two-storey villa. The home of a calligrapher and seal carver tends to resemble his brush and knife - every tree and blade of grass in the courtyard seems quiet and refined.

The former residence of Sha Menghai stands at No. 15 Longyou Road, Hangzhou, covering 870 square metres with a total floor area of 601 square metres, a two-storey villa of brick-and-timber construction. The five-character plaque reading 'Former Residence of Sha Menghai' in the courtyard was written by the seal carver and calligrapher Qian Juntao. It formally opened to visitors in November 2004.

Sha Menghai (11 June 1900 - 10 October 1992) was a celebrated Chinese calligrapher and seal carver. Originally named Sha Wenruo, with the courtesy name Menghai, he came from Sha village, Tangxi township, Yin County, Zhejiang (today's Yinzhou District, Ningbo). In his later years his ties to the Zhejiang Museum ran deep, and his former residence lies in a quiet courtyard on Longyou Road in Hangzhou.

562b8103-e326-55c2-8d20-d775b1f9f5d2.name: The Former Residence of Sha Menghai on Longyou Road

blocks.text: In the Leifeng Pagoda gallery at the Gushan Campus, let your eye rest first on those small, exquisite Asoka pagodas: study the 'mountain-flower banana-leaf' corners and the engraved scenes on the bodies, then reflect that they once stood at the centre of the underground palace of Leifeng Pagoda - a little pagoda is a chapter of the Buddhist kingdom of Wuyue.

Leifeng Pagoda was built under the direction of King Qian Chu of Wuyue in the Five Dynasties, enshrining a relic said to be the Buddha's spiral hair. The underground palace, directly below the pagoda's central chamber, was opened on 11 March 2001. It was a brick-built vertical shaft with an iron reliquary casket at its centre. The underground palace yielded 51 groups of artefacts; among them, the gilded pure-silver Asoka Pagoda is one of the most important objects from the site, its body holding a golden container that presumably enshrined the Buddha's spiral-hair relic.

Most of the many artefacts unearthed at Leifeng Pagoda in 2000-2001 are now collected and displayed at the Zhejiang Museum. Both Asoka pagodas are square in form, composed of a base, a body, four banana-leaf 'mountain flowers' and a spire, with scenes from the Buddha's jataka stories engraved on all four sides of the body.

Gongchen Bridge spans the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal and is the emblematic old bridge of the canal's Hangzhou section. Standing on the bridge and gazing at the water, you are looking at a thousand-year waterway linking Beijing and Hangzhou. The Grand Canal runs from Tongzhou, Beijing, in the north to Hangzhou in the south, 1,794 kilometers in length.

The Grand Canal links the five great river systems of the Hai, Yellow, Huai, Yangtze, and Qiantang. Its origins trace back to the late Spring and Autumn period, to the Hangou cut by King Fuchai of Wu — the earliest stretch of the Grand Canal with a firmly dated beginning.

In the Sui dynasty the north-south Grand Canal, some 2,700 kilometers long and centering on Luoyang, was dug; rebuilt in the Yuan dynasty, it became the Grand Canal as it is today. In 2014 the Beijing–Hangzhou Grand Canal was inscribed on the World Heritage List as part of the Grand Canal.
Standing beside Gongchen Bridge, hold on to two facts — Beijing to Hangzhou, and the linking of five river systems — and you have grasped the basic frame of this canal.

Walking along the canal in Hangzhou is walking through a history of grain transport (caoyun). Caoyun was a specialized system of moving public grain by river or sea routes, and Chinese histories recorded it as early as the Qin and Han eras.

After the Sui reunified north and south, several sections of canal centering on Luoyang were dug in succession, known in history as the north-south Grand Canal; the Yuan emperor Kublai rebuilt the canal on the foundations of the Sui-Tang waterway, cutting straight through its bends, and the Yuan astronomer Guo Shoujing oversaw the digging of the Tonghui River.

Before sea transport and modern overland routes arose, the Grand Canal generally handled about three-quarters of the nation's freight; in the Ming and Qing dynasties a special grain transport directorate was even established at Huai'an. After the Yellow River changed course in 1855, the canal's Shandong section gradually silted up, and once the Tianjin–Pukou Railway opened in 1911 the Grand Canal's importance collapsed.

To remember the Grand Canal, keep in mind its 1,794 kilometers and the five river systems it links — every one of its bends is tied to more than a thousand years of grain transport between north and south China.

In the Liangzhu Museum galleries, let your eye settle on the King Jade Cong, square without and round within. First study the beast-mask motifs that cover its surface, then consider how this great object, unearthed from Tomb 12 at Fanshan alone, came to hold the 'king's' place in the jade ritual system.

The King Jade Cong was excavated from Tomb 12 at Fanshan. Weighing 3,500 grams and carved with exceptionally fine beast-mask motifs, it is regarded by scholars as the 'King of Cong'; the same tomb also yielded a jade yue regarded as the 'King of Yue'. The cong is a ritual object for worshipping the earth, square outside and round within, and the Liangzhu cong is considered a passage linking the gods of heaven and earth.

These 'kings of jade' also appear in the collection of the Zhejiang Provincial Museum, and the King Jade Cong itself is on the list of relics prohibited from travelling abroad. In the museum, take note of the panels near the case explaining the Fanshan royal tombs, and read the tombs and the objects together.

'Square outside is the earth, round within is heaven' — if you remember only one thing at the museum, remember the name 'King Jade Cong' and the cosmic square-and-circle it holds, and you will have grasped the heart of Liangzhu jade ritual.

In the ceramics gallery of the Gushan main building, take the phrase 'jade fragments from Mount Kun' as your cue for this stretch of exhibits: from the Yue kiln's 'like jade, like ice' to the powder blue and plum green of Longquan, comparing the glazes as you go is a shortcut to understanding the celadon of Zhejiang.

The permanent exhibition 'Jade Fragments from Mount Kun - A Showcase of Ancient Chinese Ceramics' is housed in the ceramics gallery of the Gushan main building, with a display area of more than 1,200 square metres and nearly 400 ceramic artefacts on view.

The Yue kiln was a porcelain kiln of Shaoxing's Yue Prefecture in Zhejiang during the Tang and Five Dynasties, with its main sites around Shanglin Lake in Cixi. In his Classic of Tea, the Tang writer Lu Yu wrote: 'For bowls, Yue Prefecture is the finest. Its porcelain resembles jade and ice.' In the late Tang and Five Dynasties, the finest Yue celadon, green as 'a thousand peaks', was reserved exclusively as tribute and so was called 'secret colour'. The Longquan kiln, by improving its glaze recipes, created unprecedented shades such as powder blue and plum green, and is generally held to have reached its golden age in the Southern Song.

blocks.text: At the centre of the site park stands a rectangular high terrace, about 670 metres east–west and 450 metres north–south — the Mojiaoshan terrace. Standing on it, you can clearly see how it rises 9 to 15 metres above the surrounding plain.

The Mojiaoshan terrace covers about 30 hectares and was built entirely by hand, requiring an estimated 500,000 cubic metres of earth and some 10,000 people. Yan Wenming believed this may have been the capital of the Liangzhu 'kingdom'.

Walk around the terrace and, from the surrounding plain, trace with your eyes how the palatial zone, the inner city and the outer city step downward in sequence — and feel the layout of the capital of 'China's first city'.

'A high and mighty artificial terrace — precisely the centre of an early state that could mobilize ten thousand people.' Gazing at the grass and wind on the open terrace, you will slowly come to understand this sentence.

When you come to the Gushan Campus, first treat it as a 'museum within a garden': walk west to the foot of the Wenglan Pavilion, stand where the lake and hills meet the pavilion, and see how a museum can coexist almost without a boundary with the scenery of West Lake.

The Gushan Campus is the oldest campus of the Zhejiang Museum, at the southern foot of Solitary Hill by West Lake in Hangzhou, adjoining the Bai Causeway and 'Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake' to the east and the Xiling Seal Art Society to the west. Completed in the autumn of 1993 and covering 20,400 square metres, its buildings form the layout of 'a museum in a garden, a garden in a museum'. It also includes the Zhejiang West Lake Art Museum and the Wenglan Pavilion.

The Wenglan Pavilion stands on the west side of the campus. Built in 1783 (the 48th year of the Qianlong reign), it was one of the seven imperial pavilions holding copies of the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (Siku Quanshu) in the Qing dynasty. Destroyed by fire in 1861 (the 11th year of the Xianfeng reign) and rebuilt in 1880 (the 6th year of the Guangxu reign), it is the only survivor of the three southern pavilions. In 2001 the State Council designated it a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level; in 2006 it underwent the largest restoration since the founding of the People's Republic, and it reopened in June 2013.

babdee75-1d7d-592e-bbc7-e8b2adcbd5e1.name: A Museum in a Garden, a Garden in a Museum, and the Wenglan Pavilion

blocks.text: Faced with the astonishing number of works this old painter left behind in the memorial room, first think what the sheer quantity means: he gave his life's effort to Zhejiang and became one of the great pillars of the Zhejiang Museum's collection.

After Huang Binhong's death, his family, honouring his last wish, donated all his more than five thousand works and over ten thousand artefacts, manuscripts and other belongings to the Zhejiang Museum, forming an important source of the museum's painting and calligraphy collection.

On 22 March 1955, Huang Binhong's family donated his collections to the museum: 1,848 titles of books, 2,416 letters, 810 manuscripts, 10 genealogies, 65 records of painting appraisal at the Palace Museum and 6 volumes of decipherings of ancient seals. In March 1958, the Zhejiang Museum established the 'Huang Binhong Memorial Room'.

bdf9a18b-f88b-5397-b4c8-51aa27f44a16.name: Five Thousand Works and the Memorial Room

blocks.text: Jiayuguan lies in a narrow defile between the Qilian and Longshou mountains. First built in the Ming dynasty, it is the westernmost pass of the Ming Great Wall and is known as the 'First Great Pass Under Heaven'.

The Ming Great Wall runs 8,851.8 kilometers from Jiayuguan in Gansu to Hushan in Liaoning, and Jiayuguan is the western terminus of that wall. In the wall's beacon system, signals warned of border incursions: smoke by day was called feng, and fire by night su.

Its counterpart is Shanhaiguan, the first pass at the eastern end of the Ming Great Wall, known as the 'First Pass Under Heaven'. In 1987 the Great Wall was inscribed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site.
Visiting Jiayuguan, remember two superlatives: it is the westernmost pass of the Ming Great Wall and the 'First Great Pass Under Heaven'.

At the Zhijiang Campus, take 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture' as your main thread for reading Zhejiang's whole history. As you enter, first remember 'three galleries, one road through ten thousand years'; then walk from the prehistory on the first floor up to the modern era on the second, and finally make a point of turning back to examine the five national treasures barred from overseas exhibition. That is all it takes to tie the whole visit together.

The Zhijiang Campus is the new main venue of the Zhejiang Museum, located in the Zhijiang Cultural Center and open to the public since 29 August 2023, covering about 54,400 square metres with a floor area of 100,000 square metres. The permanent exhibition 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang - A Showcase of Zhejiang's History and Culture' occupies the first and second floors, divided into three galleries - 'From Prehistory to the Sui and Tang Dynasties', 'Wuyue and the Two Song Dynasties', and 'From the Yuan, Ming and Qing Dynasties to the Modern Era' - tracing Zhejiang's history from the Paleolithic to 1921. It opened in August 2023.

All five groups of artefacts from the Zhejiang Museum on the list barred from overseas exhibition are found in this one exhibition. In other words, walk the length of 'Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang' and you will see all five national treasures in a single visit.

cc5357fc-e089-511d-9166-86cdb144adef.name: Ten Thousand Years of Zhejiang and the Five National Treasures

blocks.text: Standing before Sha Menghai's former residence, widen your view to the Zhejiang Museum: the relationship between this master's calligraphy and seal carving and the museum can be read in a life packed with posts and responsibilities.

Sha Menghai's ties to the Zhejiang Museum ran deep: in August 1953 he became concurrently head of the museum's history department, and in August 1984 he was appointed honorary director. He also became a professor of calligraphy and seal carving at the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts in 1963, was elected director of the Xiling Seal Art Society in 1979, and served as head of the Xiling Academy of Calligraphy and Painting in 1980.

Sha Menghai kept close company with the other great names of the Zhejiang Museum, and his works, together with those of Huang Binhong and Wu Changshuo, make up the museum's holdings of painting, calligraphy and seals. As you look at these works in the galleries, you will see how calligraphy, seal carving and the cultural institutions of Zhejiang are bound together in one bond of destiny.

cde3c3cc-de7a-5299-a660-3e868432c3bb.name: Calligraphy, Seal Carving and the Zhejiang Museum

blocks.text: Standing before the memorial room at No. 31 Qixia Ridge, first picture an 85-year-old man coming south in the summer of 1948: it was here that he lived out the last seven years of his life. Look at the paintings and inscriptions inside, and connect these works with those 'last seven years' to feel the mood of his late creative life.

The Huang Binhong Memorial Room stands at No. 31 Qixia Ridge, Hangzhou. In the summer of 1948, the 85-year-old Huang, invited by the National Hangzhou Academy of Fine Arts, came south from Beiping and spent the last seven years of his life here. The memorial room formally opened to visitors in 1988.

Huang Binhong (27 January 1865 - 25 March 1955) was a modern Chinese landscape painter. He died on 25 March 1955 and was buried in the Nanshan Cemetery in Hangzhou. Today a Huang Binhong memorial hall stands at the foot of Qixia Ridge, and the Huang Binhong Art Museum and Huang Binhong Park have been built in Jinhua.

blocks.text: The Yaoshan Archaeological Site Park lies about 5 kilometres northeast of the ancient Liangzhu city. At the centre of the site is a square altar aligned exactly north–south, used for major rituals before becoming an aristocratic cemetery when it fell out of use.

The altar was originally a terrace 20 metres square and 2 metres high, from whose surface twelve jade-bearing tombs were cleared. Lying south of the altar in two rows, the tombs are all rectangular shaft graves with heads facing due south; the cemetery may also be connected with astronomical observation and calendar-keeping. This is a space intimately bound up with sacred authority and ritual.

In February 1989, Yaoshan and Fanshan were both named among China's Top Ten Archaeological Discoveries of the Seventh Five-Year Plan period. As an altar and a cemetery in one, it embodies the union of 'jade, ritual and power' in Liangzhu society.

When you visit Yaoshan, first find the square outline of the altar, then look south across the neatly aligned tomb pits — sacred altar and the dead share one place, the most direct page of Liangzhu's theocratic power.
